en: Kalyāṇavarman’s *Catuṣpīṭhapañjikā*: A Formatted Diplomatic Edition o[1]o+ Homage to all the Ḍākinīs!
Upon his head, he bears the image of a Buddha, with the crescent moon shining above the sun; and on his body are Maitreya of beautiful form and Mañjughoṣa of excellent physique.

Having prostrated before the fivefold embodiment—Vajrin, who arises from the lotus, whose body is like a staff yet bent and curved, who possesses a terrifying roar, who is consciousness itself in the form of primordial wisdom, who has destroyed the fear of cyclic existence—(I offer this homage). || i ||
This Pañjikā, which elucidates the hidden knots of the illustrious *Pīṭhamahātantra*, is now being written at the request of Senavarman. II.

From the words "Thus spoken" (*evam bhāṣita*) up to the statement "overflowing with joy" (*abhyandann iti*), the case endings, genders, numbers, compounds, and so forth—as well as the heavy and light syllables, pauses (*yati*), meters, and so on—should be applied appropriately according to the requirements of the meaning.

1.1.1 By the passage beginning with "Thus spoken by the Omniscient One" (*evam bhāṣita sarvajña*), four topics are indicated, whether explicitly mentioned or implied: the teacher (*deśaka*), the manner of teaching (*deśanāprakāra*), the object to be taught (*deśya artha*), and the locus (*sthāna*).

In this context, "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*) refers to the teacher; "thus" (*evam*) refers to the manner of teaching; "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the subject matter to be taught; "pure abode" (*śuddhāvāsaka*) refers to the location; "therein" (*tatra*) refers to the meaning of the term; "of the sages" (*ṛṣīṇām*) means "of the Buddhas"; and although it is sometimes written as "of the seers" (*ṛṣīṇām*), the meaning remains the same. Regarding "Yoginījālasaṃvara": the *yoginīs* are the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and so forth; the *jāla* (net) is a collection; and *saṃvara* is that which repeatedly (*śatśat*) chooses (*vṛnute*) or partakes (*bhajate*) bliss (*sukham*). Thus, it is the "Yoginījālasaṃvara."

1.1.2 Regarding the phrase "taught in the assembly" (*pariṣadi deśitavān*), he says "the ascetic qualities" (*dhutaguṇa*) and so forth. The reading *dhutaguṇaḥ* also exists in both [manuscripts]. In both cases, [the assembly consists of] Maitreya, Bhīṣma, Vajrapāṇi, Lambaka, Samantabhadra, Trigaṇḍaka, Gaganagañja, Meru, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Meruśikhara, Kṣitigarbha, Padma, Lokeśvara, Padmodara, Prajñātīkṣṇa, and others such as these, up to including gods and humans.

1.1.4 *Jñānendra* means their lord (*īśvara*), so to speak; *rahayogasya* means in the secret convention (*guhyasamaya*); *sundari* refers to the earth. 1.1.5 *Ānāpānāsya śvāsānām* means of the breaths of inhalation and exhalation; *ūrddhvagāmivāyūnāṃ rāṣṭradehādidevānām* refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). The sense faculties, their objects, the elements (*dhātu*), and the bases (*āyatana*) are included. *Jñānavijñānam*: knowledge (*jñāna*) is based upon the person (*puruṣa*); consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the form of the deity, which is wisdom (*prajñā*).

1.1.6 Desiring first to teach the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*), which serves as the means for all ritual procedures, he says "Listen," and states the division of breaths that constitutes one of these two:

1.1.7 "Twenty thousand," and so forth. "Twenty thousand" (*ayuta*) means ten thousand; "two" refers to two tens of thousands. "Thousands" means one thousand; "six hundred" means six hundreds. "Sixty *ghaṭikās*" means sixty *ghaṭikās*. The meaning is that in each respective day and night there are this many breaths. 1.1.8 "Hāra" is exhalation (*praśvāsa*); "dolā" is inhalation (*ucchvāsa*).

1.1.9 It should remain marked externally. "The twelve-fold world (*bhuvanadvādaśaka*) likewise" means: therein, "world" refers to the twelve-fold wheel, that is, a grid of twelve squares. "Externally" means having written it on the outside; "it should remain marked" means that the numerical syllables (*aṅkākṣara*) should be placed. This means that the twelve [squares] beginning with Rohitā, which are measured externally according to the sequence of the directions by means of the numbers starting from 'm', should be placed within the twelve-fold grid.

Regarding the question of from which day that sequence of days should begin, he says: "Starting with Pauṣa. This means beginning with Pauṣa, the month of Puṣya, up until Mṛgaśīrṣa. [The names] beginning with Rohitā and ending with Kāma are to be placed in the twelve outer squares; this is what is meant. According to the teacher's instruction, the twelve links beginning with ignorance (avidyā) are expressed by these alternative synonyms, starting with Rohita.
1.1.13: "The red [deity] is to be worshipped with seven [verses] for the sake of longevity; likewise, 'so be it'. This is to be explained according to the principle of the *kārikā*. 1.1.57:
Regarding "having expelled," the characteristic of the mouth and body—that a state of ease arises through the cessation of natural activity—is to be understood everywhere.

1.1.58: Regarding the rule *siddhir vṛṣabha-rephāṇām*, [it means that] whatever task is being performed under the asterism Vṛṣabha, under Rohiṇī, under Makara, under Raṇḍā, or under Mṛgaśiras, that succeeds; this is the meaning. As for the statement "calculated in the forenoon, O wise one," the counting of one's own asterism and so forth should be performed starting from the time of dawn until such time as [the activity is undertaken]. 1.1.65: Regarding the passage beginning with *vāsukī rohiṇī kṣetre*, etc., in the examination of a bite and at the time of administering an antidote, one should apply Vāsuki and the others to the asterisms of Rohiṇī and so forth; this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the phrase "one should specifically understand this application of the sequence of the poison" (1.1.68), the word *asya* refers to the previously mentioned Nāgacakra. "Of the application of the sequence" (*kramayogasya*) means that the specific distinction between what is curable and incurable must be understood according to the sequence. He states this very point: "The yoga born from the Siddhis, Vṛṣabhas, and Rephas is [called] Amṛta. Here, the word *siddhi* is a synonym for inauspiciousness. The meaning is this: when bitten in a Vṛṣabha or in the four Rephas, the end of that person's life occurs; therefore, it is said that "the yoga born from the Amṛta arises," which means that the victim becomes one whose time has come (i.e., dies).

1.1.69 “By applying the procedure otherwise through the yoga of poison-removal”: this means that if one is bitten by a snake other than the four *repha*-snakes mentioned in the *Vṛṣabha* [chapter], then the treatment is as follows. 1.1.70 “The seasonal course beginning with Pauṣa, according to the movement of the Sun, is the northern course (*uttara*): This means that according to the sequence of months starting from Pauṣa, based on the movement of the Sun, there is the seasonal course known as the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) and the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*). The term “northern” refers to the northern course; during the southern course the days increase, while during the northern course the nights increase—this is the sense.

1.1.71 Now, he explains the increase and decrease of the sixty *ghaṭī*s (units of time) through the division of day and night for the twelve months beginning with Puṣya, starting with "ten, double, and four," and so forth. "Ten, double, and four" means that in the month of Puṣya, during the day, there are twenty-four *ghaṭī*s. For that same month, at night, "ten, three, and likewise six" means thirty-six *ghaṭī*s.

1.1.72 Regarding the phrase "having made [the calculation] day by day" up to the completion of the month: in this very manner, the division of *ghaṭikās* for each individual day, both by day and by night, is to be understood. Regarding the second square (1.1.73), for the month of Māgha:
"ten doubled for the sixth" means twenty-six *ghaṭikās* by day; "ten tripled for four" means twenty-four *ghaṭikās* for that same [month] at night.

1.1.74 “Ten times eightfold” means that in the month of Phālguna, there are twenty-eight *ghaṭikās* by day; “ten times threefold plus two” means that its night consists of thirty-two *ghaṭikās*. 1.1.75 “In the middle of the equinox, the pair is joined” means that in the month of Caitra, thirty *ghaṭikās* are established; the meaning is that there are thirty *ghaṭikās* both by night and by day.
1.1.76 “Ten by three, twofold” means that in the month of Vaiśākha, there are thirty-two *ghaṭikās* during the day; “ten times eightfold” means that its night consists of twenty-eight *ghaṭikās*.

1.1.77 Ten times three for the month of Jyeṣṭha: there are thirty-four *ghaṭikās* by day. Ten times two for the sixth [month]: thus, in its night there are twenty-six *ghaṭikās*. 1.1.78 Ten times three for the sixth [month]: in the month of Āṣāḍha there are twenty-six *ghaṭikās* by day. Ten times two for four: the meaning is that in its night there are twenty-four *ghaṭikās*.

1.1.79 Thus he states that the conclusion of what is called the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*)—which is the cause of the increase by day—is reached at the end of [Āṣāḍha], beginning with "the southern course," etc.

1.1.80 Desiring to state the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), which is the cause for the increase of the night, he says: "Ten, tripled," and so forth; "ten, tripled, four" means that during the day of the month of Śrāvaṇa there are thirty-four *ghaṭikās*. "Ten, doubled, sixth" means that during the night of that same month there are twenty-six *ghaṭikās*.

1.1.81 "Ten, tripled, two" means that during the day of the month of Bhādrapada there are thirty-two *ghaṭikās*. "Ten, doubled, eighth" means that during the night of that same month there are twenty-eight *ghaṭikās*.

1.1.82 "Ten multiplied by three shall be the measure for the *lakṣya*": this means that in the month named *Aśvina*, which is the equinox (*viṣuva*), there are thirty *ghaṭikās* both by day and by night. 1.1.83 "Ten multiplied by two for the eighth": in the month of Kārttika, there are twenty-eight *ghaṭikās* by day; "ten multiplied by three for the second" refers to its night, which has thirty-two *ghaṭikās*.

1.1.84 *daśa dviguṇa ṣaṣṭhasya* etc.: In the month of Āgrahāyaṇa, there are twenty-six *ghaṭikās* by day; *daśa triguṇa catvāraḥ* etc., meaning that during the night of that same month, there are twenty-four *ghaṭikās*. 1.1.86 Furthermore, having raised the doubt as to how many of their respective positions (*svāsānāṃ*) exist within a single *ghaṭikā* among those [positions] divided according to the divisions of night, day, and so forth, he says: *daśa trika tathā ṣaṣṭhī* etc. Here, the meaning is as follows: regarding the number of sixty *ghaṭikās*, within a single *ghaṭikā* of that very day-and-night (*ahorātra*), there are three hundred and sixty [units].

1.1.87 Just as there is a sequence for the months—such as [the month of] Āsāḍha and so forth—in the same manner, the sequence of ghaṭikās and breaths proceeds in its entirety according to the order of the months beginning with Puṣya. Regarding the *cchinnikā*: during the equinoxes of Citrā and Aśvinī, the movement occurs in fullness throughout day and night; for the remaining [months], the movement proceeds through decrease and increase by way of being *cchinnikā*.

1.1.88 Having explained the divisions of the breath (*śvāsa*) and *ghaṭikā* according to the divisions of the vehicles (*yāna*) and the months (*māsa*), he now speaks in order to determine the division of the number of days in a year: "Kharādityādi" and so forth. "Kharādi" refers to twenty-four; "kharādi" refers to six ending with the letter *ḍha*, because in the *Ārṣimātrikā* the reading is "yavaralety ṛtum," thus making exactly six. Having combined all of this together, it is marked by the two vehicles (*yānadvaya*).

The meaning of "having then divided the two vehicles into two" is that one should divide this basis—which is a mass consisting of thirty-six units—into equal parts; thus, in each single part, there would not be eighteen numbers.

1.1.89 "Having multiplied by ten for each of the two": there, having multiplied each of the two parts by ten, one should combine both; whatever number is obtained, that many days and *ghaṭikās* are determined in the year. The meaning is that there are also breaths (*śvāsa*) within a *ghaṭikā*. It should be joined with its numerical value: by the numerical value of that day of the year and the numerical value of the *ghaṭikā*, the breaths of the year are to be made manifest through their digits.
That is what is to be known.

1.1.90 Having thus explained the measure of the *nāḍīs*, the wheels (*cakra*), the year, the month, the day, and the *ghaṭī* in terms of breaths, [the author], desiring to demonstrate the *yogicakra* for the purpose of observing the signs of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness according to the divisions of the Lord (*Īśvara*) established within the twelve external wheels, says: "Having grasped the Lords in the sentence," and so forth. This is the instruction here: in a clean place smeared with fallen cow-dung, within a mandala fashioned from sandalwood, saffron, and other substances...

Having drawn a wheel of twelve squares with chalk consecrated by the seed-syllable of Pañcaḍākinī, one should write therein the vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *aḥ*, including the neuter vowels, while omitting *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*. Then, having personally performed a salutation to one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and having taken the measure of the vowel in the questioner’s statement, one should again take the letter of the wheel indicated by that number.

That number is multiplied by three, and [the digit] is further multiplied by six; having added sixty-five to that very [product], one should determine the auspicious or inauspicious [result] by observing the sequence of the remainder left after dividing by twelve. The meaning is "excluding the neuter vowels and so forth" and "excluding ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ.

From the beginning of this section, starting with "The attainment of the sequence of the letter *a*," up to the end of "and taking the final [vowel]," he explains the observation of the sequence of causal factors (*nimittānusaṃsā*).

1.1.102. Now, regarding the statement "having grasped the vowels within the sentence" (90a), the Blessed One himself spoke in order to clarify the instruction therein: "The six-fold mark should be placed," and so forth. "Six-fold" means six times. This is the meaning: one should establish the sixfold mark for as many vowels as there are in the questioner's sentence. To the question, "How many types of [vowels] are there for the establishment of the sixfold [mark]? he says: "Of the three groups of three in the preceding [set]," which refers to the very vowels of the questioner's sentence.
The meaning is that one should first multiply by three and afterwards multiply by six.

He says again: "This mixed [number] is fifty-six. One should take the number already multiplied by six and mix it with fifty-six; having combined them, one should divide by the *bhuvana* (the world-number). Having divided by twelve twice, one should subtract [the quotient]. Then, "having grasped the remaining syllables": this means that one should determine the auspicious or inauspicious [result] by reflecting upon the syllable indicated by the digits remaining after the division by twelve twice.

1.1.104 With the words "of the hour-sign" (*horācihnasya*) and so forth, he again speaks regarding the types of auspicious and inauspicious signs. "The *hora*" refers to a line drawn like a cow's urine (*gomūtra*), purified by the previously mentioned consecrations (*saṃskāra*). Having drawn it with chalk empowered by the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the *ḍākinī*, one should place the twelve vowels upon the remaining syllables. The meaning is that the sequence of the vowel that has become the final one through counting must be stated. Alternatively, [the procedure continues] with the words "having cast a flower" (*puṣpaṃ nikṣipya*) and so forth.

Furthermore, he explains the very application for stating the signs: this is the instruction. Having first drawn the twelve-spoked wheel according to the previously mentioned sequence—and therein also excluding the neuter vowels—having arranged the twelve vowels, one should cast a flower preceded by the contemplation of one's desired object. In whichever square the flower falls, one should determine the auspicious or inauspicious result for that person by means of the vowel situated in that square. ||o||
Thus ends the commentary on the first chapter in the illustrious *Pīṭha*. ||o||

1.2.2 With the words "Listen, O Vajra, O Great Queen," and so forth, the Blessed One explains that very point.
1.2.3 By the mere throbbing of the breath, [in] six months [and] six months.
(MS: *ṣaṭmāsāṃ*; MS: *ṣaṭmāsaṃ*)
The passing away of embodied beings.
[Of embodied beings] MS, [of those who breathe] MS;
thus: of breaths, inhalation and exhalation, inhalation and exhalation° MS, exhalation° MS.

The occurrence of the bodily characteristics through decrease or increase in a manner contrary to the stated number is "decay and growth of the body. "Death" occurs for embodied beings merely by way of transition;
[the reading *maraṇam* is correct, while *smaraṇam* in the manuscript is an error].
"Fear" is as described by the words "some fear" and so forth. He states another sign of untimely death: "this meaning is 'some fear'."
This is the meaning:

[regarding the phrase] "having seen some kind of untimely death" (akālamaraṇaṃ dṛṣṭvā), it means that when one sees a certain premature death. Regarding "the cheek with the joint throbbing" (kapolaṃ ghūrṇasandhikam), it means that the cheek becomes one where the joint is quivering.

1.2.4 Regarding "if, in calamities, by mere breath, 'it is cut, it is cut'" (āpatsu yadi mātreṇa śvāsāc chidyate chidyate): in calamities, even when death has not reached its appointed time, if it is counted merely by the measure of the breath—by the mere measure of the breath.
[By the knower] it is cut,
it is cut; [there is] growth.
When there is increase and decrease, then one dies; in that regard, this is the sequence of cutting off.

Regarding thorough knowledge, the instruction of the Guru is as follows: having prepared twelve compartments provided with two rims, one should write [the numbers] in the central compartment. Therein, in the outer compartment according to the rule, the number five (5) is in the first compartment; in the second compartment, ten (10); in the third compartment, fifteen (15); in the fourth compartment, twenty (20); in the fifth, twenty-five (25); in the sixth, twenty-six (26); in the seventh, twenty-seven (27); in the eighth, twenty-eight (28); in the ninth, twenty-nine (29); and in the tenth, thirty (30)—this last is indicated by a letter-number.

In the eleventh [cell], thirty-one (31); in the twelfth, thirty-two (32); in the middle [cell], thirty-three (33). By this, the sequence of the breaths is to be known. Again, in the first cell of the middle rim, three years (3); in the second, two (2); in the third, one (1).

In the first [month], one [day]; in the fourth, six months; in the fifth, three months; in the sixth, two months; in the seventh, one month; in the eighth, one fortnight (15 days); in the ninth, ten days; in the tenth, five days; in the eleventh, three days; in the twelfth, two days; in the middle [period], one day. By this, the years and months of life are [reckoned].
And it was further stated in verse that for twenty-five days, one ascends by increments of five for each successive day.
