[the gain is] MS. The points, multiplied by the lunar days, directions, and arrows, are the lifespan in verses.

Thus [it is said]. And at what time should these, which have been transferred through the process of decrease and increase by way of five *ghaṭikās*, be examined? To this he says: "In the forenoon, the Rohita portion. The meaning of this is that one should examine them when the Rohita limb has arrived in the morning.

1.2.5 Now, based on the cutting of the channels (*nāḍī*) established in eight parts, he states the measure of the days of life: "In the nose, monthly," and so forth. This is the meaning: if there is looseness of the flesh at the tip of the nose, one dies in seven days; from the cutting of the space of the eye, death occurs in five days.
[Regarding the *pañcāhika*:

In the same way, due to the severing of the channel called *troṭā* in the sky of the eye, because of its lack of pulsation, it should be recognized as [fatal] after five days; and that [channel], throbbing at the base of the nose and the outer corner of the eye, [is likewise fatal]. 1.2.6 "By means of the cheek, however, [one knows the death] of those on the sides"—that is, from below the ear down to the jaw.

And regarding the channel (*nāḍī*) at the side of the *hanoś*: upon its severance, there is one night [of life remaining]; this is due to the interruption of the *uḍaka* [channel]. From the ear-cavity (*karṇṇasaṃkulikā*).

When the channel attached to that [tongue] is severed, there are five *ghaṭikās*—this is the "tongue-time" (*jihvākāla*) sūtra. Upon seeing a black line on the tongue like a thread suddenly appearing, there are two nights. Regarding "attached to tooth and tooth," when the teeth are joined together, there are likewise two nights.
1.2.8 On the side of the neck.

On the side [of the neck], the vessel called *manyā* is located externally; upon its severance, [death occurs] after half a month. Regarding those [vessels] situated in the hollows of the heart-cage, upon their sudden collapse into the heart-cage, [death occurs] within a fortnight. 1.2.9 Nakhāśroṇita.
“Of bodies” means:
[7] suddenly.
"Of the nails of the hands and feet, suddenly"— that is to say, when the redness of the hands and feet has suddenly vanished, for exactly six days,
the aforementioned symptoms [occur] during this untimely period.

He explains the method of protection for a person characterized by the signs of death: "One should cut the mental [channels]," he says. This instruction applies everywhere—in whatever place a channel is severed—one should meditate upon the deity produced from the seed-syllable as stated in that very location. He states this very point: "One should press with the wisdom-seed-syllable. The wisdom-seed-syllable is the syllable *HŪṂ*.

The seed-syllable of Vajrī is *hūṃ*; the seed-syllable of Ghorī is *sūṃ*; the seed-syllable of Vetālī is *kṣūṃ*; the seed-syllable of Caṇḍālī is *yūṃ*; the seed-syllable of Śiṅghī is *hūṃ*; the seed-syllable of Vyāghrī is *smryūṃ*; the seed-syllable of Jaṃbukī is *ymryūṃ*; and the seed-syllable of Ulūkī is *kṣmryūṃ*.

Furthermore, for the sake of protecting that very [mandala], he describes the procedure for establishing the outer wheel, beginning with the words "I shall describe another protection. Regarding the phrase "taking two unbaked vessels," this refers to two raw earthen saucers.
Having taken the two [substances], one should write with *rocanā* and saffron; there is an option [to use] either *rocanā* or saffron. 1.2.16 Now, where the wheel—
[Regarding *cakra*: The manuscript (MS) says "ka°";
he describes the manner of writing it as "of the nine-square section and so forth. This instruction is: [8] a nine-square [grid] wrapped with a single rim on a lower bowl (*adhasarāva*).

A wheel consisting of nine squares is to be drawn; that is to say, "above, like twelve parts" means that even on the upper *sarāva* one should draw a wheel of twelve squares encircled by a single rim. Now, he states the instruction for the *vidarbha*: "one should draw."

One should write [the name of the person to be accomplished], according to the passage beginning with "the name of the one in the middle" (madhyasya nāmam). One should write the name of the person to be accomplished in the center of both bowls. To the question of how one should write it, he says: "in that way, by means of the encirclement of seed-syllables. The meaning is that one should write it after interlacing it with the syllables of the mantra.
In order to clarify that very point: 1.2.17.

In order to clarify [this], he says: "The salutation preceded by the *svara*. The *svara* of salutation is the syllable *oṃ*. One should write that before the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). From the words of protection, i.e., from the words "protect, protect" (*rakṣa rakṣa*), one should write the name of the person to be accomplished before them. "But at the end of the seed-syllable" means immediately after that which was just mentioned. At the end, one should write the syllable *hūṃ*, adorned with the five Buddhas.

1.2.18 *Hutākṣaraṃ tasyeti*: At the end of that [mantra] adorned by the five Buddhas, one should place the syllable of the oblation, namely the word *svāhā*. Thus he describes the arrangement of the middle [section], having interlaced it, as the rim-circumference (*nemivalaya*). Regarding the phrase "the vowels with the upward and downward [sounds]," this refers to the upper rim-circumference (*ūrdhvanemivalaya*).
[Regarding] *valaya*:
it is to be understood that one should place the twelve vowels, excluding the neuter ones, in both [circles]. Now, he states the seed-syllables to be placed in the nine squares within the lower bowl:
[8] *khaphā*...

Regarding the phrase "of the double seed-syllable of *kha* and *pha*": *kha* is earth, its seed-syllable is *hūṃ*; *ha* is wind, its seed-syllable is *yuṃ*; the double [of that] is *kṣuṃ*; and by the name of the Vajra deity, it is *suṃ*.
Thus, the *hūṃ* syllable is conjoined with these five. [This occurs] in the midst of all of these.

In accordance with the sequence of *koṣṭha-vidarbhaṇa* (the method of interlacing), he speaks in order to indicate *vidarbhaṇa*: "The final [syllable] of the measure and the invocation" (*pramāṇāhutāntima*). This application is as follows: *oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa suṃ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā*. In this way, it is to be interlaced (*vidarbhanīya*). Likewise, it should be applied to the syllables beginning with *kṣuṃ* and so forth. It has been stated that the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is adorned by the five Buddhas and joined with the five *suṃ*s. To explain that, he says: "The staff, Lokeśvara," and so on. By means of this verse, *huṃ*...

The syllable *hūṃ* has been explained; and that which is the "staff" (*daṇḍa*) is the straight line beneath the letter *ha*, and that is Lokeśvara. The "crooked" (*kuṭila*) is the vowel *ū* within the syllable *hūṃ*, and that is Vajrapāṇi.

1.2.20 The letter *ha* is the limb; he is Mañjunātha. The bell is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Because these two possess a single nature, there arises the conceptual distinction as to whether the letter *ha* has the nature of Mañjuśrī or the nature of the Perfection of Wisdom. Maitreya is at the head, signifying "so it is. That which is the line forming the head of the letter *ha* is Maitreya. Regarding the letter *ma*: "The letter *ma* indeed has a blazing crest; therein is the letter *ma*. This refers to the line in the shape of a half-moon that blazes upward, upward.

*M* is the bindu at the end of that; those two are the "liberators from saṃsāra. *Vairocana*. 1.2.21–22. He now states the arrangement of the seed-syllables beginning with *kha*, according to the sequence of the grid (*koṣṭha*), starting with the words "established in the east, northeast," and so forth. Therein, in the eastern grid, [the syllable] *sūṃ sūṃ* (MS, *saṃ*).

Vajraḍākinī in the north; Ghorāḍākinī at *kṣuṃ* in the west; Vetālī at *yuṃ* in the south; Caṇḍālī at *huṃ* in the east. Thus is the arrangement of the directions. 1.2.23. Now, [the arrangement of] the intermediate directions... [MS, vig° MS].

He states the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*): "And likewise *Siṃhinī* in the northeast. One should place *smryūṃ Siṃhinī* in the northeast square; *hmryūṃ Vyāghrī* in the southeast corner; *ymryūṃ Jaṃbukī* in the southwest square; and *kṣmryūṃ Ulūkī* in the northwest. One should install [them there].

1.2.24 Regarding these very seed-syllables of the corners, he speaks in order to explain their own form: "the four syllables. This is the meaning: having established the four syllables as *sa*, *kṣa*, *ya*, and *ha*, one should place the letter *ma* beneath them; beneath that, the letter *ra*; beneath that, *la*; beneath that, *pi* (which stands for *ya*); and beneath that, the vowel *ū*. Above all of these, one should write a half-moon (*ardhacandra*) joined with a bindu. When this is done, the four [syllables] beginning with *sa* are each joined with six letters.
Thus it is. With this much, the instruction on the lower series wheel (adhasarāvacakra) is complete.

Now, he gives the instruction on the arrangement of the seed-syllables for the upper series wheel (ūrdhvasarāvacakra), beginning with "the twelve places in the east" and so forth. This is the meaning: regarding the previously mentioned twelve-compartment wheel, in the cardinal directions, ending with the *praṇāma* and *āhuti* [mantras]. As before, it is joined with the interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) starting from the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*;
[9] the neuter [seed-syllable] is joined.

"One should establish the neuter"—one should establish the four neuter vowels: *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*. 1.2.26 Regarding these very neuters, you have spoken of them by way of their nature as *ḍāginī* and so forth; therein, *ṛ* is *dīpinī*, *ḷ* is *cūṣiṇī*, *ḹ* is *kambojī*, and *ṝ* is *ḍāginī*.
1.2.27 Now, [I shall explain] these according to their application.

He states the sequence of arrangement by means of reasoning: "The place [is marked] with *ḍākinīs* in the east," and so forth. One should place *ṛ* and *ḍākinī* in the eastern square; *ṝ* and *dvīpinī* in the north; *ḷ* and *cūṣiṇī* in the west; and *ḹ* and *kaṃbojī* in the south. Furthermore, the arrangement according to the teacher’s tradition regarding the corners is described: *ī* and *ī̃* in the two squares of the northeast corner; *u* and *ū̃* in the two squares of the southeast corner; and [the same for] the southwest corner.
The placement [of the syllables] is as follows: *e* and *ai* in the two central squares; *o* and *au* in the two squares of the northwest corner.

1.2.28 By the words "having written the name in the middle" and so forth, [the author] reminds us of the interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) within the central square like a wheel, as well as the arrangement of the letters in the outer rim and the surrounding circle.

1.2.30 It is said that the letter *m* within the wheel should be visualized as being inscribed (*evalikhita*). "Presided over by the five Ḍākinīs" means it is presided over by the five Ḍākinīs; that very wheel is what should be visualized. To the question of what kind of nature the teacher (*ācārya*) should visualize himself as, he says: "The self of the yoga-holder of Vajra. This is the instruction: having performed the yoga of Vajrasattva according to the sequence stated in the *Maṇḍalopāyikā*, one should recite "I am Vajrasattva" (*vajrasatvo 'ham*) or "Vajrasattva, ha ha [10] m.
The meaning is that, having assumed this ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*), one should perform the visualization.

1.2.31–34. Regarding "with the tip of the hand holding a vajra": having performed the yoga of Vajrasattva according to the stated sequence, one visualizes a five-pronged vajra on the palm of one's own hand; with that, one should touch the vessel. Having recited the seed-syllable *hūṃ* eight hundred times as stated in the middle [of the rite], and having worshipped with [mantras] such as *gatvā* and so forth, and having offered the *bhūtabali*, one places it at the head of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This is the procedure for the external protection.

1.2.35 Now, in order to demonstrate the auspicious and inauspicious [results] for those who inquire about omens based on the equality or inequality of the location and the practitioner’s own composure (*svāsa*), he says: "Furthermore, by one's own composure," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "all success is declared" (*sarvasiddhiṃ tu kathyate*), it is by means of "composure" (*samasvāsena*).
"With an even breath," [MS], "with an equal breath," [MS];
having approached, he who inquires about the signs [approaches] the teacher, [MS], the noble one, [MS].

Standing on the right side, one should observe what is auspicious according to the flow of the right channel (*nāḍī*) when he asks; however, if he stands on the left and asks, one should observe it according to the flow of the [left] channel.
[Regarding the reading *pravṛttyā* in the manuscript (MS) and *pratyā* in the manuscript (MS): 1.2.36 To demonstrate that very point, he says: *śubham*.
He said:
"On the right, the right," and so forth. This means that during exhalation through the right [nostril], one occupies the right position;
[alternatively,] the left position.
"Subha" means up to [verse] 1.2.37; by its opposite, [it is] the opposite. (Note:
*°viparītena* is supported by MS, while *°viparīte* is also found in MS.)

"Again, the impure, again the impure," he says; "the turning away of those who speak with confidence," and so forth. "Turning away" (*vivarta*) means proceeding in a contrary direction (*viparīta-pravṛtti*).
[In the case of] *pravṛtti*, MS; [in the case of] *pravṛttyātī*, MS;
here, *niyatam niyatam*, MS; *niyata*°, MS.

When the right inhalation (*dakṣiṇasvāsa*) occurs, the left position is inauspicious; when the left inhalation (*vāmasvāsa*) occurs, the right position is inauspicious. Even when the inhalations are equal in their respective positions, [the result] is determined by the distinction between the necklace (*hāra*) and the swing (*dolā*). Demonstrating this according to the specific nature of the desired or undesired object, he says: "At the moment of the yoga of the breath," and so forth. "Moment" (*kṣaṇa*) refers to the necklace-inhalation (*hārasvāsa*); "breath" (*prāṇa*) refers to the swing-inhalation (*dolāsvāsa*). Even though the two inhalation-positions may be in the same place, if one asks while in the necklace-position, that is auspicious; when one asks while in the swing-position, it is otherwise.

1.2.38 He explains that very point: "In the [moment] of all rites, it is nourishing (*pauṣṭika*)," and so forth. The intention is that by being "nourishing," there is the accomplishment of all ritual goals.

1.2.39 Now, in order to teach the protection of those bitten and the application for the removal of poison, he says: "Those bitten by poison," and so forth. In that context, "treatment" (cikitsā) means that treatment should be administered. 1.2.40 Again, "the fourfold application," etc.
[MS, catuyogādi].

Regarding the passage beginning with *daṣṭasya* (of the bitten one), etc.: "In the fourfold conjunction" (*caturyoga*) means there are four *repha*s; for those [bitten by the snakes] therein, no medical treatment (*cikitsā*) should be performed. The connection is that for those bitten elsewhere than that, there is treatment. He illuminates this very point with the words beginning with *cikitsānyatra sarva* (treatment elsewhere is all...).

Having thus stated the section on the summary of the bitten, and desiring to state the medical treatment preceded by protection for what has been summarized, he first explains the protection with the words beginning with *nyased akṣaravinyāsaṃ* (one should place the arrangement of syllables). In that context, [the mantra is] eight-syllabled (*aṣṭākṣara*). *MS: aṣṭākṣara; MS: daṣṭākṣara* (Note: The manuscript reading *daṣṭākṣara* is corrected to *aṣṭākṣara* based on the context and the provided variant).

The placement [of the mantra] upon the limbs is the method of protection (*rakṣāvidhāna*). This is the eight-syllable mantra. These eight syllables of the mantra—beginning with *suṃ* and so forth—are the eight ḍākinīs who have become the mantra itself.
[The seed-syllables of the ḍākinīs]: Regarding their placement upon the eight limbs: there is the yellow syllable *kṣuṃ* on the head;
[it is] yellow. MS, *pītaṃ*. MS, *pītaṃ*. MS.
The two eyes are blue *hūṃ* syllables.
Blue;
[in] both ears.
The nose, the nose— [in] the two.
And on the two [eyes], a red syllable *yuṃ*;
on the tongue, the syllable *suṃ*.

On the tongue is the white syllable *suṃ*. These are the eight seed-syllables of the Ḍākinīs, beginning with *suṃ*, which constitute the mantra. Their placement on the eight limbs is as follows: on the head is the yellow *kṣuṃ*; on the two eyes is the blue *huṃ*; on the two ears and the two nostrils is the red *yuṃ*; on the tongue is the white *suṃ*; on the neck is *smryūṃ*, which is white tinged with yellow; [MS, hmryūṃ MS] *hmryūṃ*;
and at the roots of the two arms is *ymryūṃ*, which is black tinged with white.
*Ymryūṃ*:

[MS, *ymryūṃ* MS] red, interpenetrated by black, on the chest; *kṣmryūṃ*, yellow, interpenetrated by red, at the navel. Having first placed these very [syllables] joined with their respective hands in their proper locations, one should then, in the section concerning the removal of poison, visualize all of them as having become white; this is the settled conclusion. 1.2.42 He says that very thing: "white-colored."
Having reflected with the seed-syllables of Hari, one neutralizes poison; thus, having protected the auspiciousness,
[one attains] wisdom after wisdom.
He speaks of protection:
even within the arrangement of the maṇḍala.

"Knowledge and consciousness are paralyzed"—this refers to the location of the central mandala, namely the region of the heart's void. With this mantra, "Oṃ kamalābhe svāhā," and with the lotus mudrā characterized by the fire-oblation (homa), one should visualize the heart of the victim as being situated in the cross-legged posture. Above that, one should contemplate a moon disc produced from the syllable *A*, and above that, the seed-syllable *Tāṃ*, which is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Knowledge and consciousness are paralyzed; knowledge is the syllable *Hūṃ*, and consciousness is also that very same thing.
Therefore, this is the meaning: consciousness, having become a star (tārakībhūta) through the two *hūṃ* syllables which constitute wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*).
[11] If, by means of the two [hands] standing at the sides of consciousness and having become white, one were to press that very consciousness—
[thinking] "I shall press, I shall press"— MS, *pīḍayet* MS.

Instruction: 1.2.43–46ab. Now he explains the medical treatment, beginning with the words "merely protected by the limbs" (*aṅgarakṣitamātra*) and so forth. In that regard, this is the method: having taken a vessel of clay or a vessel of copper and the like, and having filled it completely with milk and water, one should place it at the base of the feet of the person bitten and also in front of oneself. In the middle of that [vessel], relying upon an eight-petaled lotus empowered by the previously mentioned mantra and mudrā, one should visualize a moon-maṇḍala above it marked with the syllable *A*, and above that as well, a vajra produced from the transformation of the syllable *Suṃ*.

Within its pericarp, having emitted from the mouths of its rays the entire circle of ḍākinīs with the sound *suṃkāraṃ*, and having withdrawn them again—having recited the mantra: *oṃ vajraśuddhāḥ sarvadharmā vajraśuddho ’ham*—[one should visualize her] transformed from that vajra.

One should visualize her as white, with two arms, seated upon a corpse in the *satvaparyaṅka* posture, with disheveled hair, adorned with ornaments of snakes, wearing a white upper garment and a lower robe, attended by a white parasol, holding a skull-cup and a *khaṭvāṅga* staff in her left and right hands respectively, seated upon a lotus petal, and having made a seat from the massed heads of the eight serpents beginning with Vāsuki.

1.2.46ab–48. Regarding the arrangement of the *nāgas*: one should place Vāsuki on the eastern petal, Takṣaka on the northern petal, Karkoṭaka on the western, Padma on the southern, Mahāpadma in the northeast, Śaṅkhapāla in the southeast, Kulikapāla in the southwest, and Hulūṇḍaka in the northwest. These [deities] possess colors identical to the eight seed-syllables (*bīja*) placed upon the eight limbs as previously described. This very point is stated by the passage beginning with "the two vessels filled with water," and so forth.

1.2.49 By means of the previously performed yoga of Vajrasattva alone—and not by any other yoga—the Noble One indicates that all of this is to be practiced. Regarding one’s own body, however, one should contemplate Vajrasattva by means of the vajra; here too, this is the case.
This is the instruction;

[it may be practiced] either according to the sequence stated in the *Sādhana* in detail, or instantaneously (*jhaṭiti*). One should meditate upon oneself as Vajrasattva. In that regard, what is called "instantaneous form" is as follows: through the transformation of the form of a vajra, which is fully perfected from the letter *A* situated within the moon at one's heart, there is the taking of Mahāmudrā as the support. Alternatively, there is the instantaneous taking of Mahāmudrā as the support.

1.2.50 Thus, having performed the mental visualization of the deity, he explains by means of the phrase "with a peacock's feather" and so forth, in what sequence the removal of poison is to be performed by the yogin. Herein the sequence is as follows: having visualized the peacock's feather in one's own hand as being held in the hand of the Jñāna-Ḍākinī, one should draw out the poison from every limb, starting from the crown of the victim's head down to the soles of the feet; then, one should contemplate the Jñāna-Ḍākinī casting it into the midst of water. This is the meaning.

1.2.51 All this must be performed by the preceptor using only the seed-syllable that has been recited. He states the mantra to be recited: *oṃ hrīṣ ṭaṭaṇḍara hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. The meaning is that at the time of recitation, this alone—the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) of the eight Nāga kings beginning with Vāsuki—is to be recited, without the interlacing of names (*nāmavidarbhaṇa*).

1.2.52 Regarding this heart-mantra, he explains by what yoga it is to be recited and its extent: "By Vajrasattva, etc."—this is the meaning. At the time of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one who has performed the yoga of Vajrasattva should recite it one hundred thousand times; thus it says, "one should recite."

1.2.61 Furthermore, he clarifies this very mantra by means of name-interlacing (*nāmavidarbhaṇa*): *oṃ hrīṣ ṭaṭṭaṇḍara ṭaṭṭaṇḍara hūṃ 3 phaṭ 3 amukaṃ nirviṣaṃ kuru hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. In this same manner, it should be applied to Vāsuki and the others as well.

1.2.62: In the phrase "mixed with white mustard and white flowers" (*sarṣapasvetapuṣpāṇāṃ tu miśritam*), the word *sve* (white) is connected with each [term]. [The commentary notes: "With sandalwood, with sandalwood"—in the manuscript (*MS*) it is *candanena*, and in the manuscript (*MS*) it is *candane*. [The gloss explains: "In this [passage], the word 'white' (*sveta*) is connected to each [of the preceding items]."

1.2.63 "By the mere movement in the heart" means that the knowledge [of the enemy] is paralyzed. By the striking just mentioned, the sense-organ moved in the heart by the life-force (jīva) should be paralyzed by the previously stated seed-syllable (bīja). 1.2.64 "By the mere throbbing of one's own breath" means one should press with one's own breath. One should interweave (vidarbha) the breath of the target with one's own breath; this is the method for the life-force and senses of the target. This means one should press them with the seed-syllable of air (vāyu-bīja).

1.2.65–66: "One should cause the self to sing with all limbs trembling"—the meaning is that one should effect the descent of knowledge (*jñānāveśana*) upon the subject (*sādhya*) by means of a song consisting of the syllable *hūṃ*. 1.2.67: "Having withdrawn [it], [one should place it] in the locations of the *nāgas*. One should cause its milk to flow; the milk and other ritual implements should be cast into the locations of the *nāgas*, such as great rivers and the like.
1.2.69: Regarding the examination of the bitten person, he states the section on non-treatment: "In the mouth, [the appearance of] sesame seeds, eyes," and so forth.

1.2.70. Having known the mental reflection of Vajrapāṇi, who was desirous of speaking for the sake of others, the Blessed One, wishing to speak himself, said: "Listen, O Great King, to the supreme *varṣāpaṇa*," and so forth. [It should be performed] in a delightful place near water. The *varṣāpaṇa* maṇḍala must be drawn in close proximity to water; not elsewhere.
"Not elsewhere" means up to that point.

Regarding the phrase "square, with four doors, adorned by eight nāgas": the meaning is that one should fashion the arrangement of the eight nāgas, beginning with Vāsuki, using five-colored powders. As for the phrase "with two heads at the door": the layout of the door must be made in the form of the hoods of both nāgas. Furthermore, the corners should be fashioned by encircling them with the two tails.
1.2.73–76ab *aṣṭaprākārabhāgasyeti*— by means of the eight snakes beginning with Jayabhadra, [one constructs] each successive enclosure wall (*prākāra*) starting from the first enclosure wall.

"One should [place] the family in the directions, the eighth in the center," and so forth; by this he teaches the arrangement in the middle. Regarding that, the instruction is as follows: having drawn an eight-petalled lotus in the center of the maṇḍala, there—on the eastern petal is Vāsuki, white in color; to the north is Takṣaka, yellow; to the west is Karkoṭaka, red; to the south is Padma, black; in the northeast is Mahāpadma, white-yellow; in the southeast corner is Śaṅkhapāla, white-black; in the southwest is Kulikapāla, red-black.

The *huluṇḍaka* of Vāyu is yellowish-red; in this way, the son of noble family should observe the distinctions of color even in the case of the ramparts and so forth. 1.2.76cd–77. *meghesvara* MS, *meghasvara* MS.

"Having drawn forth the eight regions of the great kingdom" means that one should draw them forth from the eight directions for the sake of the great cloud-gods (*mahāmeghadeva*). "Resounding, swirling, terrible, and indeed with whirling clouds, [accompanied by] the filling of fierce rain"—these are the kings of the great clouds; their mantras are to be understood according to their respective order.
1.2.78–81. He states that very same thing in the sixth case: "Having established the eastern direction, one should meditate upon the color of the directions. This is it. [13] ø ø.

The author states that all this must be performed by the yogin through the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) with Vajraḍākinī: "In the center, the Vajraḍākinīs are seated upon lotus-thrones. One should employ a serpent as the seat for the lotus that is entwined by serpents; [the deity] is situated on a lotus-throne entwined by snakes. Regarding Vajraḍākinī, one should visualize the Great Cloud King (*Mahāmegharāja*) issuing commands via the eight *piṅga* nāgas. To clarify that very point, [the text says]: "The yogin [should realize] inconceivable gnosis (*jñāna*) as the gnosis-ḍākinīs through the self-mantras.
1.2.8–83 *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā*. This is the mantra for the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*).
1.2.84–92: *Oṃ vāsuki hūṃ svāhā*. In this manner, [the mantras] for Takṣaka and the others should be applied.
1.2.93–94: *Oṃ ghili 2 varṣa varṣāpaya hūṃ 3 svāhā*. This is the mantra for the eight kings of clouds (*aṣṭamegharāja*).
1.2.99–100: *Oṃ varṣa bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā*. This is the mantra to be recited (*japyamantra*). These are the mantras for Vāsuki and the others.

1.2.102–103: This explains that all of this must be performed by the yogin who has already attained the signs (*labdhanimitta*). Furthermore, it says "he will explain the signs that have been produced" (*kṛtanimitta*), and so forth. "Kekara" means a slight impairment of the eyes.
1.2.104 Just as in the case of a messenger, there is a reason for a twofold examination; the meaning is that one should examine oneself by means of the messenger.
1.2. Thus ends the second chapter in the *Catuṣpīṭha-pañjikā*. ||~||o~||

1.3.1 Thinking that the accomplishment of mantras and so forth does not occur for one who has not generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), [the author], beginning with the words "O Blessed One, I wish to hear the commencement of yoga" (*bhagavan śrotum icchāmi yogārambham*) and "especially," begins the third [chapter on] the mind of awakening; [he does so] beginning with the words "First, having contemplated emptiness" (*prathamaṃ śūnyaṃ saṃcintya*).
1.3.2 Regarding those who have ascertained all phenomena, it is said:

[14] Form, form-emptiness, and so forth; first, regarding the eight [elements], "mind" refers to the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the phenomenon-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*). This should be applied similarly to the eye and the other [senses]. "The elements of form are empty" means that form is empty of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The meaning [is as follows]:
"One should cause only that which is concealed (saṃvṛta) to be performed"—this means it should be understood to apply even to sound and the other sense objects.
1.3.8: "The mind dissolves into space" (līyate mana ākāśam); the intended sense is that one should contemplate the mind as space. And it has been said:
Place yourself within the verse, and place the void within yourself; having known the interval between the two, he who sees thus is liberated.
Verse 1.3.9: Of the three realms—desire, form, and formlessness.
Verse 1.3.11: "But they see its middle."

Regarding "tv ity" [MS], "tvi tv ity" [MS]: here, "asya" refers to the examination of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). In that context, "kāraṇam" means one should examine the sign (*nimitta*) which indicates the desirable or undesirable; this is the meaning. With "pradīpena tu sānni syād," he states the signs such as proximity (*santika*) and so forth. Regarding "rajarajaṃ tu pauṣṭikam," here "rajaḥ" means dust (*reṇu*); subsequently, the yoga arises. With "aṅkudibhiś cetanetyādinā," he explains the experience of the fruit of the signs.
1.3.15 “One should observe the course of the objects of knowledge”—this is to be understood from the instruction of the Guru.

1.3.16 In this section, in order to clarify the very suchness (*tathatā*) already explained, he says: “Having killed mother and father,” and so forth. Here, “mother” is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and “father” is delusion (*moha*). “The king” is the ego-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*); “the two Vedic scholars” refers to the sense-faculties beginning with hearing; “the kingdom” is the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) together with their attendants, namely conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and the consciousnesses that are the result of conceptualization (*vikalpavijñāna*). “Having killed” means their slaying by means of the sword of wisdom (*prajñā-khaḍga*) alone.
"Battle," so it is said. ||~||~o||~|||
Thus ends the third chapter, on Emptiness, in the *Catuspīṭhapañjikā*. ॐ.

1.4.1–2 Thus, for a yogin who relies upon suchness (*tathatā*), there is no accomplishment of ritual action (*karmasiddhi*) without the ego-identification with the deity (*devatāhaṃkāra*). Desiring to explain the yoga of the deity, as well as [rites of] paralyzing, slaying, and so forth, the Blessed One begins the fourth chapter with the words, "Listen to the reality according to the path," and so on, starting with "free from duality and non-duality. The meaning is that it is devoid of unity and plurality. By means of the "enemies of water" (*jalaśatruka*), there is the crossing over for those sinking into the ocean of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) due to passion and the like.

[Regarding *uttaraṇam*: MS reads *uttaram*. He says: "For those whose bodies are situated in the middle, that which is to be brought forth is called the *lakṣa*. Regarding the phrase "of the *lakṣas*, *lakṣaṇas*, and *lakṣaṇās*": *lakṣya* is Mudgala; *lakṣaṇa* is the means (*upāya*); *lakṣaṇā* means the state of intention (*abhiprāyatā*). [In the passage] "the wise one, by means of knowledge, in the mind"—here, regarding "in the mind" (*cetasi*)—MS reads *cetasyety atra*.

In consciousness, there is the grasping by a cognition of the object characterized by another cognition, as well as the grasping of the characteristic and the mental activity; thus it is stated in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*: [text fragment].
By the *citta* karma is accumulated, by the *manas* it is conceptualized,
and by the *vijñāna* one discerns.
In order to clarify this very point, [the author] says: "Having perceived the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should observe the course of all that is to be known" (1.4.3).

Regarding the phrase "one among a thousand yogis has attained the course of former births" (1.4.4), the term "course of former births" refers here to the path of the Tathāgatas. This is the intended meaning: that among hundreds of thousands of yogis, not even one attains it—or at least, so it is said.

1.4.5 Regarding one whose body [of defilements] such as passion has been completely eliminated through the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he says that the planting of the seed to be described must be performed:
"the empty field," and so forth.

[Regarding the phrase] *kṣetrādi*: "The wise man [should perform] the sowing of the seed in the body" (1.4.6). This very point is further nourished by the passage beginning with "Just as in the houses of the Mātaṅgas," and so forth. In that context, let the excellence (*prakarṣa*) of the abode of the gods and others be stated; let this meaning be established: just as a dwelling of outcasts (*caṇḍāla*), once burnt, is made into a temple for the gods and others, so too the body presided over by the elements (*gāra*, etc. is completely consumed by the fire of knowledge for the sake of sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "the planting of the seed of the *dharmadhātu* must be performed for the production of a body sustained by genuine compassion, [performed] by the wise belonging to the noble family": here, "noble family" refers to the compassionate ones, the wise practitioners (*yogins*); the meaning is that compassion and the like must be generated by them.

This is stated in the passage beginning with "one should place the arrangement of syllables" (*nyased akṣaravinyāsam*), where he speaks of the placement of the seed-syllable (*bījavinyāsa*). Regarding the line "one should imagine fire above," one should place the syllable *kṣum* on the head; this is the eye of the seed-syllable of the earth-duality.
[Of that very one] MS;
[of this one] MS; "one should apply" MS, "one should apply" MS; "yojaditi" MS.

One should place the syllable *huṃ* at the eyes (1.4.8), which is the seed-syllable of wind (*vāyu*) and space (*śūnya*). With the mind, one should contemplate the syllable *yuṃ* at the nose and the ears; that is, one should meditate on the syllable *yuṃ* at the nose and the ears. [The syllable *am*], the seed-syllable of water (*ambu*), [should be placed] at the tongue—at the tongue.
The Lord should place the syllable *suṃ* upon the tongue as the Īśvara.
(1.4.9–10) [Regarding the phrase] "of whom," it begins with *suṃ*, beginning with *suṃ*.
(MS, suṃkārādiṃ suṃkārādiṃ; MS, suṃkādirādiṃ)

The meaning is that these very [syllables] are to be grasped in their secret form (*kūṭarūpa*). One should apply them in four places: *smryūṃ* at the neck, *ymryūṃ* at the heart, and *kṣmryūṃ* at the navel. "Calculation by means of the limbs" refers to the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) performed in this manner.

1.4.11 "Of one whose body is disciplined" refers to the placement of the seed-syllables (*bījavinyāsa*) in this manner. Regarding "consisting of the Knowledge-Ḍākinīs": one should meditate upon oneself as having the nature of the Knowledge-Ḍākinī.
1.4.16 Regarding the phrase *alikāliprayogeṇa*: *ali* refers to [the vowels] beginning with *a*; *kāli* refers to [the consonants] beginning with *ka*.
1.4.17 Regarding the phrase *bhrūmadhye bindusthānam*: [the reading] *bindusthānam* [is correct];
[the variants] *°sthānam* (MS) and *°sthānām* (MS) are incorrect.
The meaning is that one should contemplate the syllable *huṃ* between the eyebrows; "adorned by the five Buddhas" refers to that very same [syllable].

1.4.18 To explain its very nature, he says: "The purpose of wind, fire, and seven. Therein, "wind" is the letter *ya*, "fire" is the letter *ra*; the unification of these two is "wind-fire. From that, "the seventh object" is the letter *ha*. "Vajrī-bīja" is the letter *ū*, according to the statement, "The crooked one is Vajrapāṇi. "Bindu and nāda" refers to the line of the *bindu* situated within the form of the half-moon; one should place this above that, as it is said to be "completely pervaded. "Dhārāvarṣa" (rain-shower) is so called because its intrinsic nature is the flowing of nectar.

1.4.20 Regarding the phrase "the eight [rites] beginning with *karman* for the former," here "the eight *karmans*" refers to: pacifying (*śāntika*), prospering (*pauṣṭika*), subduing (*vaśya*), and malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). By the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), paralyzing (*stambhana*), deluding (*mohana*), and possession (*āveśa*) are included. Furthermore, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the sword (*khaḍga*), the underworld (*pātāla*), the vetāla, magical deception (*kuhaka*), collyrium (*añjana*), the *roṇā*, the *siddhārtha*, and the *tālaka* are also understood.

"Then the *tālakā* [MS], the *tāla* [MS], the *gerī*, the *paṭala*, and others as desired. Regarding "prior service," this refers to recitation (*japa*) and meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*); here too, by the word "etc.," vows, observances, fasting, and so forth are included.
1.4.21: "Listen, O Vajra!"—with these words, he explains the extraction of the mantra according to its true nature and so on. Regarding the phrase "of the preceding Vajra-sentence":
In the phrase "pūrvvasya," [the reading is] "pūrvvasyeti" in MS;
in the phrase "vajravākya," [the reading is] "vākyeti" in MS.
The word *vajra* refers to the first sound; "first" here signifies the beginning of a group (*varga*). Thus, the letter *ka* is the first of its group.

According to the rule "of the fourth of each group" (1.4.22), taking the *ka*-group, there is the selection of the letter *ta*, which is the fourth of its own group. "Doubled" means a *repha* (the letter *r*) is placed above; thus, it is a conjunction of two *t*s. "A *repha* above" means that a *repha* should be placed upon the head of that very letter. "The *repha* joined to the *i*" means a *repha* conjoined with the letter *i*.

1.4.23 “According to the class, the second [syllable] with two syllables and a dot” means that the letter *cha* together with the *anusvāra* (ṃ) is [the first part]. “Of that very one, pressed by a hook, the letter *i* should be given” means that the letter *i* should be added to that same [letter *cha*]. “The third of the fourth” refers to the letter *da*. 1.4.24 “Having pronounced the pair twice” means a double repetition of *n* and *dha*. “But conjoined with the fifth” means joined with the fifth, the syllable *hūṃ*; that is to say, it is embraced or accepted by it. “[Preceded by the syllable of salutation]”:
[MS reads] *°pūrvvasyeti*; [another reading is] *°pūrva + ti*.

The intention is that one should first place the syllable *oṃ*. At the end of each [syllable], following the final letter, one should place the syllable *phaṭ*. This is the application: *oṃ vajrakarttari*.
°karttari] MS, °karttiri MS:

*cchinda* 2 *hūṃ phaṭ*. 1.4.25: Having formed the *vajrabandhana* with the two hands well-joined (*susaṃmiśram*), one should apply it to that which is being consumed; thus it should be placed upon the opening of the mouth.

1.4.26 "Having extended [the fingers] in the middle of the *krodha* [mudrā]" means: having spread both the index and middle fingers, one should perform cutting many times with the form of a *kartarī* by touching [the object] repeatedly.

1.4.27 Now, with the words "I shall explain the pillar [and] the pillar-stopping," and so forth, he teaches the stopping of rain and other phenomena. Therein also is the extraction of the mantra: according to the rule that the last letters of each group are taken as three syllables, the letter *va* is selected.

1.4.28 Regarding the third [letter] of each group: "It is grasped by three syllables" refers to the letter *ḍa*. "By the letter *e*, the third part of the preceding [group] is formed by means of seed-syllables" refers to the letter *va* conjoined with *e*. 1.4.29 Regarding the fifth [letter] of the preceding [group]: "One should press it with a hook" refers to the letter *pa* joined with *i*. "The syllable of the middle [group] is the visarga" refers to the letter *va*. "But the seed of the thunderbolt (*vajrībīja*) is near" refers to the letter *ha*. 1.4.30 "By the side of the hook" refers to the letter *ra*. Below that very [letter], the letter *ra* should be adorned with the letter *ī* on its head.
[It is] to be performed;
at the end of the syllables for destruction (*ghātākṣara*), one should place the syllable *phaṭ*. *Praṇamā praṇamā*. (Note: MS reads *praṇamā praṇamā*; another manuscript reads *pramāṇāmā*.)

"It should be given first" means that one should first place the syllable *oṃ*. Here is the instruction: all this is to be performed by the yogi with the supreme *ahaṃkāra* (the sense of "I am"). According to the *bhūtatantra*, it should be understood as "drink, drink."
[It is] to be seen.

Having formed the *añjali* with both hands—having made the *vajrāñjali* with the two hands, [joining] the ring fingers (*anāmikā*) with the little fingers (*antaka*). Then, having pressed them together with wrath, one should encircle the two ring fingers with the two index fingers (*tarjanī*) in reverse order. Joining the middle fingers and the two thumbs constitutes the *vaḍavāmukha-mudrā*. This is the *vaḍavāmukha-mudrā*, formed by joining the two middle fingers and the two thumbs; its radiance is filled with garlands of flames.

Blazing and burning in the ten directions, let the cloud-deities and others be devoured! With splendors filled with garlands of flames, by the glorious and supreme *svāhaṃkāra*s, the cloud-deities situated in the ten directions—MS, MS:
*devatāṃ*.
They are to be seen as if they were devouring; such is the instruction.
1.4.col. [The word *ācārya* is found as *ācārya* in MS; it appears as *āryarya* in MS. In the *Catuṣpīṭha-pañjikā* composed by Kalyāṇavarman, the *Ātmapīṭha* is completed. ||~|| o~||

2.1.1 Now, Vajrapāṇi, desiring to understand how the production of the reflection-image, the fire-offering (homa) for pacification and other rites, the nature of the sacrificial offering (bali), and the formal acceptance of disciples are performed, says: "O Blessed One, I wish to hear," and so forth. He [the Blessed One] then empowers the commencement of the other seats (parapīṭha).
[Note: The manuscript variants *adhiṣṭhāpayati* (MS) and *adhiṣṭhāyati* (MS) both indicate the sense of empowerment.]

2.1.3–7. Regarding the section on the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*): beginning from one cubit (*hasta*) up to one thousand [cubits], according to the requirements of the ritual, starting from eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*)—[MS:
*aṣṭāṅgulam aṣṭāṅgulam*; MS: *a + ṅgulam*]—up to [the maximum].

[Up to] twenty finger-breadths one should increase [the measurement]. Here, "altar" (vedī) refers to the collection of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa). One-third of the occupied area is to be dug out; having divided the pit as prescribed into three parts, two parts are to be excavated.
"By one-eighth of the dug-out portion, [one makes] the *kuṇḍaka*"; that is, having divided the dug-out portion into eight parts,
the altar (*vedikā*) should be made with the measurement of one of those parts.

2.1.8 One should cause the *nemi* (rim) to be made on the outer half-portion of the *oṣṭha* (lip). The external *nemi-valaya* (rim-circle) should be made with half the measure of the *vedī* (pedestal/base). The *nemi* should be joined with eight [petals]. The lotus petals should be made with eight times the measure of the eighth part of the *nemi-valaya*.
2.1.9 For the exterior of the lotus, there should be one wall (*prākāra*) of one *aṅgula* each for the lotus. [17] The lotus...

A wall of one finger-breadth should be made outside the lotus; however, within the center of the *kuṇḍa*, vajras should be placed upon the lotus, according to what is aesthetically pleasing in the middle of each *kuṇḍa*. A lotus should be laid down, and upon that, a vajra should be installed.

2.1.10–11: "But for malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), it is triangular"—thus [it is said]. For malevolent magic, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is triangular; for pacification (*śāntika*), it is square. The sacrificial pit for pacification should be made square. For subjugation (*vaśya*) or nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), the pit is circular. For eradication (*uccāṭana*) and so forth, it is shaped like a half-moon. For attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) and immobilization (*stambhana*), the pit is bow-shaped.
For immobilization, it is one-eighth [the size]. For attraction and immobilization, it is one-eighth.

The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one-eighth [of the area]; it should be applied in successive order for rites such as pacification (śānti), nourishment (puṣṭi), and subjugation (vaśa), according to the sequence exactly as stated.
The rites for pacification and so forth must be performed; not otherwise.

Regarding the statement, "One should place the symbols of the five Buddhas according to their respective directions": one should place Satvavajrī and the others in the cardinal directions by turning counter-clockwise (vāmāvartena). The arrangement therein is as follows: Satvavajrī in the eastern quarter, Ratnavajrī in the north, Dharmavajrī in the west, and Karmavajrī in the south. These symbols are to be placed upon the lip.

He says "not elsewhere": it is adorned with the mark of the Buddha at the four places, namely the lips. The moon and vajra, beautifully radiant, are to be placed even in each corner; the moon and vajra are to be placed in every corner according to their beauty, just as in the place of the seat. Kailāsa, Kailāsa.

One should place the auspicious Kailāsa altar, which has arisen [from the ground], at the front of the seat; it is joined with half a *pauruṣa* and twelve thumb-breadths (*aṅguṣṭha*). Here, "the measure of a *pauruṣa* hand" means that its half is a *vitasti*, and furthermore, together with twelve thumbs, it is four [vitastis].
It is twenty-four finger-breadths; that measure is known as *kelāsa*. 2.1.14 On the petal, with eight [units].

Regarding the eight places: the sequence is the installation of the deities and so forth. On the eight petals of the lotus, in due order, Vajraḍākinī and the others are to be installed. He says that the rule of treading upon [the seats] must necessarily be performed.
"Treading upon" means his treading upon them.
But by means of the remainder, one should cause the yogins to know. ||~o~||
2.1.col. In the *Catuṣpīṭhaloka*, the first chapter in the section on the *parapīṭha* is completed. ॐ.ॐ.ॐ.

2.2.1 Out of curiosity regarding what has been heard, the Lord Vajrapāṇi—desiring to hear about water-offerings (*udakahoma*) and so forth, such as "of what nature is the water-offering? and so on—inquires about the second chapter in the *Parapīṭha*. Water-offering (*jalahoma*) is an offering performed in waters. Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), offerings of oblations (*bali*) and gifts (*upahāra*) are included. "How is it to be known? means: what is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the water-offering like? 2.2.3 "Another water-vessel" refers to a vessel other than the aforementioned *kalaśa* and so forth. [Note: *kalaśādy* is repeated in the manuscript.]
One should smear with white sandalwood paste and other fragrances a water-vessel made of gold or other materials, which has the shape of eight lotuses.
2.2.6 [Afterwards, afterwards]:

"One should cause the external [deity] to perform the activities of water, form, and so forth. Having instantly visualized oneself as having the nature of Vajraḍākinī, afterwards, by means of the self-consecration (ātmasvāsa) according to the previously mentioned sequence of arrangement.
Having returned in due order, one should [place] the Jñāna-ḍākinī in the external location in the midst of the water, according to the sequence of karma. [18] Color.
Having produced the colors, weapons, and so forth, one should perform the fire offering (*homa*) for the sake of pacification and other purposes.
One should display them individually, just as with the *samaya-mudrās*; that is, like the *jñāna-ḍākinī-samaya-mudrā*.

One should show the handful [of water] with the *vajraḍākinī* mantra and so forth, using the universal mantra for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) specifically. For the *vajraḍākinī*s and others who have been visualized before one, great nourishment arises by offering a handful of water daily upon the crown of the head at the peak of the *vajra*. ||oṃ||
2.2.col. In the *Catuṣpīṭhaloka*, the second chapter on the *parapīṭha* is completed. Om.

2.3.1 For a yogin who has cultivated [the practice] in this way, the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasiddhi*) does not occur without the drawing of the mandala. Listen, O Great King Vajra, to the characteristics of that which lies beyond saṃsāra, and so forth—with these words, he begins the chapter on the mandala (*maṇḍalapaṭala*). Since the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvabhāvya*) of the five aggregates and so forth was explained in the chapter on emptiness (*śūnyatāpaṭala*), it is not investigated here.
2.3.5 "O Blessed One, I wish to hear," and so forth; [the phrase] "I wish to hear" and so forth has its meaning already explained.

2.3.6: "Listen, O Vajra, to the characteristic of non-dual gnosis according to its true nature," and so forth; by this, he speaks of the purification of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). 2.3.10: "Having recited these, one should cause the supreme [deity] to perform the *añjali* gesture"; the meaning is that, having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one should perform the unsurpassed worship of the Buddha.

2.3.14 “It should be joined with the syllable *hūṃ* at the end, following the strike of the *praṇava*. This means that between the strike of the *praṇava* and the end, the syllable *hūṃ* should be joined; that is to say, the mantra is *oṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Having visualized one’s own hand as a *vajra* by means of this mantra, one should perform the striking (*sphālana*) upon the five places of the Tathāgatas. Thereby, the purification of the ground is accomplished.

Then, having prepared a square maṇḍala with fragrant scents and having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with five-colored powders, one should then place, in the center, the sequence for all accomplishments; on the eastern petal, a five-colored thread; on the southern petal, a vajra; and on the northern [petal], a bell and a great conch filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and so forth.
Having drawn the mandala on the western petal of the vessel [containing] the great conch and so forth, one should completely surround the colored powder on its side,
repeatedly encircling it.

"One should establish [it]" means that immediately thereafter, the preceptor, with the pride (*ahaṃkāra*) of Jñānaḍākinī, should perform worship with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, food offerings, bali-offerings, and other such gifts.

Following that, having formed two vajra-fists with both hands and placing them inverted upon the tips of the breasts, one should extend them toward the directions and strike away the obstructors (*vighna*) with this [mantra]: *Oṃ aparasarantu bhavanto ye kecit sthānasvāminaḥ devanāga-nāga-yakṣa...* [MS].

"O Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Bhūtas, Bhūtinīs, and Ḍākinīs, depart quickly for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings! HŪṂ PHAṬ 3 SVĀHĀ. This is the mantra and mudrā for the expulsion of obstacles.
Then, having formed the Lāsyā-mudrā: "OṂ PRASĀDAṂ KURU MĀTMEBHI SUNDARĪYA YĀCITAṂ HŪṂ JRŪṂ JRAṂ SVĀHĀ. This is the mantra and mudrā for requesting the ground.
Immediately thereafter—
The verse [reads] *vajram tatvena* [MS:
*satvena*].
Having gathered [them], he should cause the ghaṇṭā to be sounded according to the Dharma.
Verse:
Then, he is established in the center of the lotus;
[he is] established. MS, vyavasthita~| MS.

Visualizing Jñānaḍākinī within the flask, white in color and holding a vajra and bell—one should then worship her. Having repeatedly formed the vajra-bond (*vajrabandha*), one should extend both index fingers, bend their tips, join them at the ends, and place it at the heart. *Oṃ aḥ svāhā* is the mantra of the heart-mudrā. With this [mudrā] together with the vajra, one should recite [the mantra] over the flasks one hundred and eight times.

Then, one should consecrate five-colored threads with the seed-syllable consisting of the essence of the five Buddhas: *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. One should recite over the five-colored powder with the seed-syllable of Siṃhinī: *oṃ smryuṃ svāhā*.

Then, having offered the bali-oblation to the spirits for the purpose of securing the site, having worshipped with the five offerings and so forth according to what is available, having brought together the ritual vase and other implements, and having placed them in the southern direction, one should appoint those engaged in the work of drawing the mandala and so forth to the ten paths of virtuous action. Then, having smeared [the ground] again with fragrant water, one should perform the laying of the lines; this is the "seizing of the site" (bhūmiparigraha).

Then one should perform the laying out of the lines (*sūtrapātana*). Having prepared nine threads of five [types], one should dye them with five colors. Subsequently, having placed a drop (*bindu*) in the center of the mandala ground and in each of the eight directions, one should again generate the pride of Jñānaḍākinī. Taking the five-colored threads with both hands joined in *añjali*, one should consecrate them with the seed-syllables of the five Ḍākinīs: *aṃ a ā aṃ ā svāhā*. This is the mantra. By the preceptor... by the preceptor. (MS, ā + ryeṇai)

Then, having grasped one end of the cord and having caused the disciple to grasp the other end, one should lay down the thread. In this regard, the procedure is as follows: while the teacher stands in the southwestern direction and the disciple stands in the northeastern direction, the teacher [should act] again.
[By the teacher] MS,
[by the noble one] MS; by the right-wandering [one] MS, by the wandering [one] MS.

At the location of Vāyu, likewise the disciple [should do so]; from the south-eastern direction by the Ācārya, in the western directions by the disciple, and in the eastern directions by the Ācārya; then at the southern location by the disciple, and likewise in the northern quarter by the disciple as well. Afterwards, one should drop the thread in the [other] directions, thereby forming a square maṇḍala. Having divided it into five parts, [one proceeds] from the central square to the second square...
One should encircle the womb-maṇḍala with a portion from the second square.
One should beautify the nine compartments with vajra-pillars, and in each corner with a viśvavajra; this applies everywhere.

One should decorate it everywhere with the fivefold division of the wheel. The gates are square; the chest [of the mandala] is half of that, and its measure is likewise. Above the chest, by half the height of the chest, is the ground for the five enclosures (*pañcaprākāra*). Within the womb [of the mandala], in the eastern, northern, western, and southern sections, one should cast the white, yellow, red, and black portions of the colored powders (*rajāṃsi*). In the centers, [one places] blue; outside the vajra-lines, in the positions of the outer yoginīs.
One should surround the area outside Pokkasādi with five walls of a deep red color; outside of that, one should apply a black-colored space, dark as the sky, and on the deity-band [MS:
*devatāpaṭṭikāyām*], one should apply a color like molten gold. These are the four outer archways (*toraṇa*). Thus it has been said:
It is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways, garlanded with rows of flaming bells, and encircled by necklaces, half-necklaces, and other ornaments.
In all the corner sections and at the joints of the door-frames,
one should fashion the outer maṇḍala in the verse by inlaying it with vajra-jewels.

Thus: on the sides of the four doors, above each kalaśa in the east, north, west, and south, one should place banners marked with a lion, a peacock, a swan, and a makara; this is the arrangement of the eight banners. One should likewise place eight kalaśas in those very places, and another set of four kalaśas in the four corners.

Such is the maṇḍala; one should draw it starting from the size of a single cubit up to a thousand cubits. Furthermore, within the maṇḍala, the rule regarding the treading upon [the ground] must necessarily be performed, just as in the case of the sacrificial fire-pit (kuṇḍa).

Now I shall describe the procedure for the ritual of casting [the ritual dagger], with the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) of Vajraḍākinī, accompanied by the sound of the syllable *HŪṂ* and together with the vajra-bell. When the task of expelling obstacles is to be performed, having made a circumambulation and a scattering of steps, standing at the eastern door with feet even, feet apart, or with the left foot bound and the right cut off, one should strike the obstacles while reciting: "I am Vajraḍākinī! By means of this: *OṂ HŪṂ HANA MĀRAYA DUṢṬĀN DUṢṬĀN*.

"Kill, kill! Aḥ aḥ hūṃ hrīḥ phaṭ! Thus [one should say]. Likewise, in the north, one who possesses the pride of Ghorāḍākinī, having formed the vajra-bind and placed it upon the heart, standing in the ālīḍha, pratyālīḍha, vaiśākha, or maṇḍala posture, should strike down the obstacles, strike down the obstacles.

~| Oṃ hūṃ āḥ phaṭ | Then, at the western gate, having formed the *lāsyā* mudrā and placing the left knee on the ground, standing in the posture of the lion-tread (*siṃhākrānta*), one should slay the obstructors with this: Oṃ āṃ phaṭ | Thereafter, in the south, with the pride of the *caṇḍālī*, having placed the vajra-bind upon the head, [standing] in the *padapada*, *kukkurapada*, *āvarttapada*, *vivarttapada*, and *vivarttapada* [postures],
one should cause the obstructors to fall with this.
[With this] MS,
[with this] MS ~ | *oṃ hūṃ āṃ phaṭ* ~ | Again, established in the eastern direction, with the very ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) of Jñānaḍākinī, [one should worship] the great form of Śrī Vajrasattva.
Having bound the great mudrā (mahāmudrā), one assumes the ālīḍha posture, the pratyālīḍha posture, and the ālīḍha-restrained posture.
(The term *ālīḍhasaṃyata* occurs twice in the manuscript.)
Standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, one should perform the *hūṃkāra*.

One should perform the ritual staking (*kīlana*) with the very mantra of the earth-purification mudrā. Extending the *vajrāñjali* at the crown of the head, one should recite this for the protective cage: *oṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Having formed the *vajrabandha*, raising the little fingers and the two thumbs, and resolving upon the directions with the *digbandhana*, one should establish the enclosure with this: *oṃ jambhani hūṃ phaṭ*.
Having placed it in the eastern flask according to its beauty, one should recite this mantra eight times while pressing the flask with the little finger and thumb of the left hand.
One should recite with this:

*oṃ tapte mahātapte svāhā*. This is the mantra for the seal (*mudrā*) of filling with the water of the Mandākinī. With that same seal and the mantra to be described, one should cast in the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and recite this the prescribed number of times: *oṃ suṃ kṣuṃ yuṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the mantra for the consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the flask (*kalaśa*).

Then, having adorned [the two] with the garments and ornaments as previously described, one who is endowed with loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables] should likewise fashion the armor (*kavaca*) for the two hands.
Having extended [the two hands], one should encircle them with the two thumbs and form the shape of a swan’s wing, rotating it within the heart.

Thus, having bound this mudrā with the application of armor—*oṃ hūṃ phaṃ phaṭ*—here too, generation begins from meditation. Having first performed the calculation of the eight limbs, one should generate the pride (*ahaṅkāra*) of Jñānaḍākinī. Then, *vajro haṃ*, thus [is] Vajrasattva.
Vajrasattva...
from the syllable *haṃ*; then the invocation, the invocation.

One should construct the maṇḍala of the Śuddhāvāsa-jñāna within one’s own heart; having drawn [the deities] into the maṇḍala, caused them to enter, bound them, and brought them under control, one should accomplish [the goal]. For each respective case, the mantras are as follows: Oṃ vajrāṅkuśa jaḥ! Oṃ vajrapāśa hūṃ! Oṃ vajrasphoṭa vaṃ! Oṃ vajraghaṇṭa hoḥ!
In the verse [mudrā],
by forming the hook-bind with the index fingers, one should press the backs of the hands together with the outer knots and tips of the little fingers, which constitute the great hook.
The verse says: The mantra for the mudrā of invocation. Thus, according to the oral instruction, is the Initial Yoga. ॐ.

2.3.15 It is said that the entire [mandala] should be visualized by the yogin who has cultivated the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) of the deity upon the summit of Mount Meru: "On the summit of Meru, one should contemplate the four castes, the directions, and so forth.

2.3.16 When this is the case, one should display the *samayamudrā*; thus it is said: "Having bound the *samayamudrās*," and so on. Having formed two vajra-fists, placing the left fist at the heart, one should place the right fist under the left armpit; this is the *samayamudrā*.
2.3.18 Just as with the seed-syllable consisting of vajra—*hūṃ*, *praṇāma*, *huta*, and *antima*—it is easy to understand. *Oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. This is the mantra of the Samayamudrā. [MS, °mantra MS].

2.3.19 It is said that the lion-throne (siṃhāsana) should be fashioned within the five compartments of the womb-mandala (*garbhamaṇḍala*). "The lion-throne itself is joined with five locations. Having visualized the solar mandala adorned with a white parasol, and so forth—it is adorned with such things as these. Up to 2.3.20: "having emerged by means of one's own breath. "And Jñānaḍākinī in the center" means that having emerged from her own seed-syllable, one should place Jñānaḍākinī upon the seat. Her three faces, six arms, and so forth are clear.

2.3.25–32. Thus, "the self departs from everywhere"—this is the water-channel (*udakanāḍī*). "The fire of the self has issued forth"—this is the fire-channel (*tejonāḍī*). "The wind of the self has issued forth, has issued forth"—this is the wind-channel (*vāyunāḍī*). "Knowledge of the earth has issued forth"—this is the earth-channel (*pṛthivīnāḍī*).

2.3.44 "But for the external ones, there is a group of four"—the meaning is that the group of four, beginning with the external Ḍākinī, should be established at the four gates, just as in the internal [mandala].
2.3.53 "By these, one should show the Vidyā and also the *samaya*. [The word *samaya* occurs twice in the manuscript. It means that one should show the *samaya* in the presence of Jñānaḍākinī.
"One should show [it]," because of the showing of that samaya before the Jñānaḍākinī. Oṃ hūṃ svāhā.

2.3.57 Regarding the phrase "of this seed-syllable joined," etc., the word *asya* ("of this") refers in all instances to that which was mentioned immediately prior. The [syllable] *daṇḍa* (the vertical stroke) has three morae (*trimātra*). Therefore, this is the ritual application: *oṃ a svāhā*, *oṃ ā svāhā*, *oṃ ā3 svāhā*, *oṃ ā3 svāhā*—this is for the four deities of the corners. *oṃ ṛ svāhā*, *oṃ ṝ svāhā*, *oṃ ḷ svāhā*, *oṃ ḹ svāhā*—this is for the deities of the inner doors. *oṃ phuṃ svāhā*, *oṃ pheṃ svāhā*, *oṃ phoṃ svāhā*, *oṃ phriṃ svāhā*—this is [for the others].
2.3.79: "Of *amṛta*, *repha*, and *bindu*": this refers to the syllable *sraṃ*. 2.3.82: "The seed ending in *na*": taking the letter *ya*, [the seed] ending in *na* is the syllable *kṣa*.
2.3.83: "Having taken the first triad of the class, one should join it with *nāda* and *biṃba*": this refers to the syllable *guṃ*.

2.3.85: "One should worship with these according to reality; thus, as will be stated later, 'one should offer the *bali* to the Daityas as before. One should present the *bhautika-bali* (elemental offering) provided with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the five hooks (*pañcāṅkuśa*), and various foods and drinks.

2.3.123–126: Having rotated the lotus-turning gesture (*kamalāvarta*), one should contemplate a lotus in the right hand and a vajra in the left; thus one should display the Great Mudrā (*mahāmudrā*). Having visualized a lotus vessel in the right hand and, with the left, the visualization of a vajra, one should form the triple-fingered mudrā (*tripatākā-mudrā*) and recite: OṂ.

Having uttered "Oṃ haḥ ho hrīḥ svāhā," the yogi should likewise contemplate this once for all around [the assembly]. This means that he should contemplate it once—just a single time—for all the yogis of the maṇḍala; he should cause it to be seen by the mind. In the section on worship, however, for the wise, there is the mundane and so forth. It has been stated that the external maṇḍala is conceptualized; this is what is meant: for those who are well-refined, the supramundane is worthy of worship.
The arrangement of the supramundane deities (*lokottaradevatāvinyāsa*): immediately after [the mundane deities],
the supramundane deities (*laukikādidevatā-devatā*).

They are to be placed in the outer maṇḍala; the sequence for their placement is as follows: outside the outer line of the inner maṇḍala, in the east, is Caṇḍī, who holds a vessel of nectar-water and is white, black, and yellow in color. In the north are Ghorī, Rudhirā, and Māṃsī, whose hands are busy holding vessels filled with the five goads and other items, and who are yellow, white, and red in color. In the west are Ugrī, Jvalitā, and Bhībhatsī, whose hands hold vessels of sacrificial offerings (bali), and who are red, yellow, and black in color.

In the south are Kapālī, Vajrī, Kumbhī, and Khādyapāṇā, who hold [their respective implements] in their hands; they are black, red, and white in color. In the northeast are Lāsyā and Gandhā, white and yellow in color. In the southeast are Vīṇā and Puṣpā, white and black in color. In the southwest are Gītā and Dhūpā, black and red. In the northwest are Nṛtyā and Dīpā, red and yellow. All of them possess a radiance filled with garlands of white flames; their hair is disheveled, they are adorned with all [ornaments], and are decorated with various garments and jewels. They are seated upon auspicious thrones (bhadra-āsana).
Then, outside [the mandala], proceeding clockwise on the ground, according to the sequence of the bali-mantras to be described:

Having conceived eight fields according to the [prescribed] rule in the eight directions, the eight lords of the fields, beginning with Kṛṣṇarudra, are to be installed there. The sequence is as follows: in the east is Kṛṣṇarudra; in the north, Mahārudra; in the west, Devadatta; in the south, Kṛṣṇa; in the northeast, Karāla; in the southeast, Bhībhatsa; in the southwest, Nandātīta; and in the northwest, Vināyaka. All of these have three eyes and four arms.

Adorned with garments and ornaments bearing the aforementioned marks, they are black, yellow, white, and red in color. In the compartments starting from the northeast (Īśāna), they are white, yellow, black, red, black, yellow, and red, together with their retinues. 2.3.149–152. In front of Kṛṣṇarudra is Cāmuṇḍī, to his left Ghorī, Bhībhatsī behind him, and Umādevī to his right; thus is the praise. His goddesses have the colors of Ḍākinī and the others, [beginning with] the five services (*pañcopacāra*). 2.3.149–152. *opacādirādi* MS, *opacārādi* MS.

With their hands busy [in offering], having worshipped with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra) and other services, there are likewise in the north Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā; these are the retinue of Mahārudra. They possess the colors of Dīpinī and the others. Likewise, in the west are Bhadrakālī and Mahākālī.

Mahākālī is the Yoginī Sthūlakālī. She is the sister of Devadatta, and her complexion is like that of a leech (*cūṣinī*). Likewise, on the right are Indrā, Candrā, Ghorā, Duṣṭā, Lambakī, and Tridaśeśvarī; these are the deities of Kṛṣṇa, and their complexions are like those of a Kambojī woman and so forth. In the northeast is Kambojī, whose complexion is like that of a *dīpinī* woman and so forth.

The *cūṣiṇīs* are the *yoginīs* residing in the village. The *ḍākinīs* of Karāla have the colors of Cāmuṇḍā and the others. In the southeast are Ghorarūpā, Mahārūpā, Daṃṣṭrarūpā, [23] and Karālinī; these are the *yoginīs* of Bhībhatsa, having the colors of the sense organs and so forth. In the southwest are Kapālamālā, Mālinī, Khaṭvāṅgī, and Maharddhikā; these are the wives of Nandātīta, having the colors of Bhadrakālī and the others. In the northwest are Khaḍgahastā, Paraśuhastā, and Vajrahastā.
*vajrahastā* MS; *dhanuhastā* MS; *viṇāyaka* MS, *viṇāyaka* MS.
The playful and non-playful goddesses, Jayā and the others, are described as follows: then, at the eastern gate, there is Hari,
the wielder of the staff (daṇḍadhara).

In the north is Brahmā, holding a chowrie; in the west is Rudra, intent on proclaiming names; in the south is Indra, holding a parasol—thus are the two divine banners. In the northeast is Śakra; in the southeast is Kuvera; in the southwest is the Lord of Spirits (Bhūtādhipati); in the northwest is the Lord of Nagas (Nāgādhipati). These are accompanied by their sons, wives, and retinues. Their colors, arms, and emblems, however, are to be understood according to the [iconographic] illustrations.

Then, on the outer altar in the eastern direction, there are Karaṅkabhairava, Khaṭvāṅgarākṣasa, Gaṇeśvara, and Ghaṇṭakarṇa; these are the colors of the Ḍākinīs and others. Likewise, in the north, there are Caṇḍeśvara, Chandodeva, Jareśvara, and Jjhāṅkārabhīṣaṇa; these are the colors of the Dīpinīs and others. Similarly, in the west, there are Ṭṭakirudra, Thaṇḍileśvara, Ḍavaruṇḍāmbara, and Ḍhakkabhayānaka; these are the colors of the Cūṣinīs and others. In the south as well, there are Tumbureśvara, Thoranāda, Daṃṣṭrākarāla, and Dhanurdha.

Thus: the colors of Kamboja and so forth. Furthermore, these have four arms; they hold a *khaṭvāṅga* and a skull-cup, embrace the Goddess, and hold a trident in their hands. They have three eyes, wear tiger-skin garments, and are adorned with all ornaments. [24] They are garlanded with a string of skulls. Then, outside, the Cakravāḍa mountains, the Bhūmis, the Pretas, Piśācas, and so forth, should be visualized as shouting "kilikila"; this is their retinue. For Kṛṣṇarudra and the others, as well as Karaṅkabhairava and the others, the first syllable of their own name is the *dharma-akṣara*. Having formed two *vajra-muṣṭis*, the index fingers...

Having extended the middle fingers in the shape of a hook (*aṅkuśa*), one should join them. *Oṃ ākarṣaya phaṭ*—this is the mantra for the mudrā of invocation (*āvāhana*) for worldly deities. With the previously mentioned mudrās and mantras for the deceased, this is the commitment mudrā (*samayamudrā*) and mantra for Pokka and the others. Having formed the hollowed palms (*saṃpuṭāñjali*), one should hold them bent toward the right. *Oṃ ghriṃ svāhā*. For Ghoryā and the others, having formed the vajra-palms (*vajrāñjali*), one should open them. *Oṃ kuru 2 svāhā*—this is for Kāpāli and the others.

Extending both hands and joining them back-to-back, one should wrap the fingertips separately. *Oṃ vattali hūṃ svāhā*. For Ugra and the others, having formed two vajra-fists, one should hold them at the junction of the hips. *Oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. This is for Lāsyā. [Apasavya, apasavya]. (MS, apavya).

Extending the thumb and pressing down with the ring finger, one should grasp it with the left hand: *oṃ supriye gandhe hūṃ* for the incense offering. With the gesture of the lute: *oṃ hūṃ ho svāhā* for the lute. One should place the joined palms (*saṃpuṭāñjali*) upon the head: *oṃ śriṃ svāhā* for the flower offering. Having formed two vajra-fists and extended the index fingers, one should move them over the mouth: *hūṃ hūṃ svāhā* for the song offering. Taking the vajra-fist, it is held at the joint of the left hand.
*Dhāritā~ | Oṃ i svāhā*—thus for the incense. Having placed the left hand tucked into the right hip region, one should hold the right hand upon the shoulder. *Oṃ sunṛtye sunṛtye*. (MS, *sunṛtyo* MS).

"svāhā"—this is for Nṛtyā; having formed the añjali mudrā, one should hold it upon the head. "oṃ kṣuṃ svāhā"—this is for Dīpā; having formed the right vajra-fist and raised the index and middle fingers, one should touch the forehead. "oṃ mu mu svāhā"—this is for Śakra; having formed the vajra-bandha mudrā, one should join the two index fingers in the shape of a jewel. "oṃ dhanāge hūṃ svāhā"—this is for Dhana; having formed the right vajra-fist with the index finger raised.

"Oṃ ghātani hūṃ phaṭ"—thus for the Lord of Spirits (*bhūtādhipati*). Having formed a right fist with the index finger fully extended—"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā"—thus for the Lord of Nagas (*nāgādhipati*). One should strike the vajra-fist upon the head. "Oṃ khe saḥ svāhā"—thus for Viṣṇu.

One should cast the southern *tṛpatā* flag onto the head with "Oṃ hūṃ svāhā"—this is for Rudra. One should move the right vajra-fist at the heart with "Oṃ svāhā"—this is for Brahmā. Extending the right hand and turning it downward, one should form the left fist and extend the wrathful fingers, snapping them in the middle in the shape of an umbrella with "Oṃ mu mu svāhā"—this is for Indra. By the very mantra of the pledge-seal (*samayamudrā*) of the Trident-bearer, [the same applies] to Kṛṣṇarudra and the others, as well as Karaṅkabhairava and the rest.

"This one too" refers to the period following the arrangement of the deities; [the author] says that one should worship the eight yoginīs, beginning with Vajraḍākinī, with twenty offerings. Afterwards, "the wise one should worship with twenty, twenty offerings" (86cd). Having formed the *lāsyā* mudrā and uttering the song of the syllable *hūṃ*, filling the air with the sound of *huṃ*, one should effect great satisfaction by means of this: *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ ghuṃ duṃ hūṃ 3 oṃ ghe 3 hūṃ svāhā*.
having grasped the vajra with its true essence (*tattva*) in the verse, one should ring the bell according to the Dharma.

The verse for this is as follows: Having formed two vajra-fists, one should join them back-to-back; having entwined the two little fingers, one should move them slightly. *Oṃ vajraghaṇṭa hoḥ | Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe raṇitapraraṇite sarvabuddhapracālite prajñāpāramitānādasvabhāve vajrasatvahṛdayāvatoṣaṇi hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā.* This is the reality (*tattva*) of the vajra-bell. Then...

O Paramādya Mahāsattva, verse.
One should offer praise with the eight hundred verses spoken by the venerable Śrī Ramādya, beginning as follows:
"Hūṃ 3! You who wear a body, you who embrace a pair, you who sustain life."
