O Bhāvavimukti, you who dwell in the secret Guhyani-kuṇḍika! Delight, delight, O Vajra! You have been pressed by the Guhyani; you must accomplish your task.
Enjoy the immeasurable and infinite, O peaceful one!
Having reflected thus,
he then offered prostrations, saying, "I take refuge in the one who brings an end to saṃsāra."

O you whose body is adorned with a white conch resting upon the head of Varuṇa and the moon, O you of immeasurable thought and beautiful form! Homage to you, O wise one; [I am] "Huṃ," having abandoned [all else].
Your golden, excellent body possesses the luster of honey.
In the most terrible Maṇḍināyā, [he is] ready for me.
Ready with skull and skull-bowl, devouring blood— victory, victory, O Sovereign Goddess Uttarī!
Beautifully adorned with an emerald hue, you roar the sound of "Hūṃ" as you become enraged at Īśa.
The terrifying and formidable Daṇḍaka-pāla has reached the western Devīna-mita-patha.
Adorned with a blue garland, having contemplated the net upon the heads of Hari and Hara, bearing the moon,
the heat of Māra, and wrath, and emitting the sound "Huṃ," bow down to me, O Destroyer of Madhu.
Having offered praise with various vajra songs and hymns such as these, one should ring the bell.

Then, placing the vajra-añjali at the heart, recite: *oṃ śuddhadharme hūṃ a ā aṃ aḥ svāhā*. Having firmly established the divine pride (*devatāhaṃkāra*), one should present the outer offering (*bāhyabali*). Adorned with the aforementioned garments and ornaments, holding the vajra and bell, accompanied by a retinue beginning with Śakra, and standing with the right foot in the sattva-paryaṅka posture while the left is extended and placed on the ground; having prepared a square mandala of fragrant paste and worshipped it with white flowers and other offerings.

One should present the offering for the eastern gate with fragrant śāli rice mixed with curd, sugar, honey, and ghee. Having formed the *ṭakkirāja-mudrā*, one should summon the deities with this [mantra]: *oṃ vattali vattali*.

*Mahāvattali hūṃ 3 jaḥ svāhā*. *Oṃ vāhanī mahāvāhinī sūryacandramukhiṃ jayavāji somarāji umadevī gaṅgā surūpī tāraya saṃgho grahaṇa sarve gaṇapati kārttika śrī śaśī devī agalo pagalo asurasurajaiḥ pukkasi mahāpukkasi hūṃ he ho ākarṣaya 2 samayādhipe hūṃ 3 phaṭ jaḥ svāhā*. With the *āvāhana-mudrā*, [touch] the *tarjanī* [finger].

With the two index fingers encircled: *Oṃ bhakṣaya 2 samaya tiṣṭha juṃ jruṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having thus satisfied [the deity] and given three snaps of the fingers, one should dismiss them; this is the *devali*.

In the mandala prepared according to the previously described rite, having arranged the offerings such as *kṣīrikā* and the like, and having placed a vessel for the oblation (*homādibhājana*) filled with a mixture of the three sweets and milk-trees (*kṣīri*), one should [invoke] outside by means of that very mudrā and mantra the following deities: Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkkoṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, Kuliśapāla, Devatī, Mahādevatī, Somaśikhi, Mahāśikhi, Daṇḍadhara, Mahādaṇḍadhara, Huluṇḍa, Nanda and Upananda, Sāgara, Mahāsāgara, Tapta, Mahātaptta, and Śrīkānti.

Mahākānti, Ratnakānti, Surūpa, Mahāsurūpa, Bhadrāhika, Mahodara, Jjhali, Mahājjhali, come, come, O Lord of Great Nāgas! *bhūr bhuvaḥ phaṭ phuḥ svāhā*. Cause the vajra-fist to be formed; having extended the left hand with the little finger and thumb joined at the tips while the middle fingers are bent like a hood, one should thus capture the nāgas and dismiss them as before. This is the *nāgabalih*.
(Note: MS reads *nāgali*...)
Then, standing facing west at the point where the mandala is to be cast,
[one should place] red sandalwood and so forth upon a triangular mandala adorned with red flowers and other offerings.
Having placed before [the deity],
as before, boiled *śāli* rice accompanied by curd and honey and joined with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and having invoked [the deity] as before: *oṃ māṇibhadra pūrṇabhadra pūrṇabhadra*.

Having performed the invocation with "Jayabhadra and so forth," and having formed the *vajrabandha* mudrā and placed it upon the heart, one should recite "dhāraye dhāraye" twice. Then, with "Oṃ dhanādhipa vattali hūṃ svāhā," one should satisfy [the deity] and likewise dismiss them; this is the *yakṣabali*.

Again, standing in the same manner facing south, having offered an oblation and so forth upon an external triangular maṇḍala sprinkled with red flowers and the like using the vajra-step and red sandalwood and other substances— with dried fish, meat, garlic, onions, blood-vessels, sesame flour, *kulmāṣa*, especially the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and various kinds of food and drink— [one should perform the ritual].

Having placed a vessel filled with *jambū* fruit together with the five nectars (*pañcasudhā*), and having invoked [the deity] by means of those very same mantra and mudrā while perceiving the vessel [as divine], one should recite "Oṃ ekavṛkṣa... and so forth. Then, having formed the Trailokyavijaya-mudrā and joined the two index fingers like a chain, one should satisfy [the deity] with "Oṃ tiṣṭha hūṃ bhakṣa 2 jaḥ phaṭ svāhā" and dismiss [them]. This is the *bhūtabali* as before.

Accompanied by the sound of cymbals and filled with the ringing of bells, one should offer the bali-oblation in the eight directions outside the boundary where the mandala ground is located, using the very mudrās and mantras for the bali-offering to the spirits.

Now I shall describe the consecration of the disciple (*śiṣyādhivāsana*). In the north-eastern quarter of the mandala, which has been smeared with fragrant scents and adorned with hanging cloth canopies and the like, and provided with the five types of offerings and so forth, one who is seated upon a lion-throne and whose nature is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) should perform the consecration. Herein is the sequence: for the sake of purifying the face of the disciple who stands before him with palms joined at the heart—Oṃ.

Having consecrated seven times with this mantra, *oṃ āḥ jihvāsaṃvarttini hūṃ phaṭ*, and having given the tooth-stick and the rice-food, one should grant the *samaya-saṃvara* as follows: "May all the Buddhas—Akṣobhya, Ratna, Lokeśa (Amitābha), Amoghasiddhi, and the rest—and all the Bodhisattvas, take heed of me! I, [name], from this very moment until I sit upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhiniṣadana*), [take up] this vow."
I generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening,
just as the Protectors of the three times have resolved upon perfect enlightenment.
The threefold training in ethical discipline and the gathering of wholesome qualities.
And I firmly undertake the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
From this day forward, I shall undertake the vow born of the yoga of the Buddha with respect to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha— the supreme and unsurpassed Three Jewels.
I truly accept the vajra, the bell, and the mudrās;
and I shall accept the master in the exalted assembly of the Great Vajra Family.
I shall bestow the fourfold gift six times every day,
at an auspicious and delightful time, within the noble Mahāratnakula, in accordance with the True Dharma.
I accept the true Dharma— the outer, secret, and triple vehicle—
within the pure Great Lotus family, which arises from great awakening.
I truly undertake the vow associated with all [beings],
performing acts of worship according to my ability. Mahā-mahā° [MS, ma° MS].
In the accumulation of the family of karma.
Having generated the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening, I have undertaken the complete vow for the sake of all sentient beings:
"I shall ferry across those who have not crossed; I shall liberate those who are not liberated."
I shall cause those who have not found rest to find rest;
I shall establish sentient beings in cessation.
In cessation,
[it is] thus.
This is the glorious, supreme path, which brings about the fruit of the Mahāyāna; by means of this, you, proceeding along it, shall become Tathāgatas.

Thus: having performed the profound teaching beginning with the *Prajñāpāramitā*, one should subsequently cause [the disciple] to enter the mandala; this is the procedure for the preparatory rite (*adhivāsana*).

Then, the preceptor, remaining within the mandala and preceded by twentyfold offerings, should salute the bell with this [mantra]. He should perform the offering of the vajra-song with the verse beginning "Haraśira-mukuṭa" (2.3.128–130).

Thereafter, having performed the fire sacrifice (*homa*) according to the previously mentioned sequence, he should take up the vajra and bell, enter the city, and—preceded by twentyfold offerings and so forth—praise [the deity] with the eight hundred names and various vajra-songs. Then he should bestow the pledge (*samaya*); thus he says: "One should cause the oyster shell and so forth to be infused with the five nectars mixed with meat. This is the meaning.

Having purified Amṛtakānti—mixed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five hooks (pañcāṅkuśa)—in the manner to be described, one should establish the commitment (samaya). Regarding this, it is said: "The syllable *ha* removes color; the syllable *ho* destroys fragrance; and the syllable *hrīḥ* is the destroyer of potency; this is the sequence prescribed. The purification of Amṛtakānti is clear. As for the instruction, "having uttered the threefold [mantra] three times, one should cause the three deities to meditate," here the threefold refers to the nature of Amitābha, Vairocana, and Akṣobhya.

"Oṃ haḥ ho hrīḥ svāhā"—thus, one should perform the recitation three times by uttering it thrice. This is the intention: having sprinkled [the object] three times with the mantra consisting of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), which arises from the seed-syllables to be mentioned, when the central [syllable] is recited, even the splendor of nectar (*amṛtakānti*) becomes meditated upon as being of the very nature of the three natures. Padmesvara, Padmesvara.

"Having the beauty of the color of form" refers to Amitābha; "fragrant water and the one who delights in existence" refers to Vairocana; "taste, Lord of the Vajra, Vajrapāṇi" refers to Akṣobhya. "One should make known by means of the three deities in a threefold way"—the meaning is that one should also meditate upon the beauty of nectar through the intrinsic nature of the three deities.

2.3.131. "In the left [hand], the moon-handed one; the syllable in the middle of the moon. On the palm of the left hand, the syllable produced from nectar (*amṛta*) arises. Having further placed the syllable of nectar upon the lunar disc, regarding the phrase "by the measure of the All-Knowing" (*sarvavid-mātra*), "All-Knowing" refers to Vairocana; his "measure" is the syllable *oṃ*. Having purified that *oṃ* with the syllable of nectar, one places that *oṃ* in the middle of the moon.

One should meditate [within the moon]; that is, within the lunar disc (*candramaṇḍalamadhye*). Regarding "the thumb is indeed the earth": one should contemplate the thumb as the earth by means of the syllable *oṃ*.

Regarding "the ring finger is Sumeru, by the power of nectar": having visualized the ring finger as Sumeru, which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of nectar, and having meditated on the syllable *suṃ* above it, one should cause the water to be churned by means of the threefold gnosis (*jñāna*). One should contemplate the water, which possesses the luster of nectar, in three ways in the center in the form of a triple-bannered flag (*tripatākākāra*).

2.3.133 "One should cause all the *yoginīs* to give their *chid-lingas* and thumbs individually"—that is, one should cause each of the *yoginīs* individually to give their *chid-lingas*. [The word *bhāvaḥ* appears twice in the manuscript. Afterward, one should cause them to perform the self-awareness through their own being—that is, one should effect the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of their own limbs.

"2.3.134 One should establish the five locations of the stūpa by means of the threefold [method]. Within the cavity of one's own shoulder-blade, upon a fully manifested lotus produced by the syllable *hrīḥ* (or *hīḥ*), one should visualize the Jñānaḍākinī, born from the syllable *hūṃ*, in the form of a caitya at the five points of the *sphoṭas*. One should bathe her three times with the falling of drops of nectar (*amṛta*) out of a desire to wash away the afflictions (*kleśa*). A wise person [should apply it] to the tip of the tongue for the three upper locations; thus, having given a drop to the tongue, the forehead, and the crown of the head, one should then give the *samaya* to the consecrated disciples."
2.3.135 By means of this verse:
Having seen this Dharma purified, one must not abandon true conviction;
for the Brahmin, the dog, and the outcaste have all been consumed within the single nature of the Self.
The disciples also, with a gesture of prostration preceded by the *kamalāvarta* [mudrā], and having formed and held the *tripatākā* [mudrā],
[should act] with this verse.
Welcome, O priceless Dharma, free from the stain of passion! Gāhāgāha.
One should avoid [wrong views] and pay homage with devotion to the truth.
Thus [it is said].

Then, having placed the disciple at the entrance of the mandala—unfumigated with perfumes and the like, holding a handful of flowers, and veiled by a face-cloth—one should administer the vows as follows:
"The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all [my misdeeds]."
I rejoice in the merit of the world; I fix my mind on the awakening of a Buddha.
Then, as previously stated: "Inherently pure..."

Having recited the purity of the three bodies (*trikāyaśuddhi*) with the words "All phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature," and so forth, and having established [the mind] in great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) and the other [immeasurables], one should perform the prostration three times.

One should perform [the following]: "Oṃ, I offer myself for the service of the worship of the five ḍākinīs; I offer myself for the service of the worship of the Ācārya; I offer myself for the protection of all sentient beings. Having thus recited this, or having performed it in three ways, and having given [it], the Ācārya should also recite three times: "You are the Samaya! Samaya! Hō! and then perform the empowerment of the Vajra of the Three Bodies.
The syllable A is the foremost of all phonemes, empowered by the vajras of speech;
the syllable I is the sign of movement, and the syllable U is the body.
Consecrated by vajras;
the syllable *hūṃ*, the wisdom produced from *hūṃ*, is consecrated by vajras in the heart.
The verse is as follows:

*Oṃ hili hili mana ghūrṇitavajracale yuṃ yuṃ yuṃ hūṃ svāhā*. "Today I am the knower among knowers; partake of the nectar. Having consecrated [the substance] three times with this mantra, *oṃ aḥ svāhā*, one should place the nectar-like radiance, mixed with the five nectars and the five hooks, into the mouth.

Then one should perform the descent [of the deity]. Having visualized in the heart of the disciple a wind-maṇḍala transformed from the syllable *yuṃ*, and having likewise placed that very same [maṇḍala] upon his feet, the preceptor—possessing the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) of Jñānaḍākinī and with the terrifying sound of the vajra-bell—should cause [the deity] to move by means of this, having issued forth a great, violent wind from his own heart: *Oṃ le le hūṃ aḥ svāhā*.
If there is no movement by this means, then [one should proceed as] previously stated, previously stated.

One should cause [the disciple] to enter by degrees. Once he has entered, one should fill him with the sound of various vajra-songs and then perform the following for the pacification of his blindness: *oṃ tiṣṭha vajra samaya pratipālite hūṃ 3 ho 3 svāhā*. Then, one should have him cast flowers. Wherever they fall, that is his deity of accomplishment. Having performed the removal of the face-cloth with *oṃ jñānacakṣuḥ hūṃ svāhā*, one should explain the reality (*tattva*) of the deities individually, such as Kāraṅka-bhairava.

Then, having shown [the mandala] ending with the Knowledge-Ḍākinī of the Rava family, the disciple—having bowed his head at the feet of the Guru and offered the arghya—should request the desired siddhi according to his name, with palms joined at the heart as before: "Oṃ, I have entered the Vajra-maṇḍala; Haṃ! [I am] the one who shows the Yoga-maṇḍala, the Great Maṇḍala."

Having recited three times, "I am initiated into the secret maṇḍala; I am the pledge (samaya), Haḥ," one should perform the eight-limbed prostration as before. Then, having generated the divine pride (*devatāhaṃkāra*) with the mantra: "Samaya Haṃ, Oṃ Vajra Haṃ Aḥ, the present Haṃ, Ho! Arisen Haṃ, A Ā Aṃ Aḥ Hūṃ Svāhā," one should recite: "The gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) is Haṃ."

For one thus established, one should bestow the consecration: the consecration of the disciple with the vase of the southern gate, the consecration of the mantra with the western [vase], and the consecration of the tantra with the northern [vase]. [The master], seated upon his throne with the grace of a universal monarch, [addresses] the disciple established in the eastern direction who has generated the mind of awakening: "Oṃ, [this is] the vajra-hook held by the vessel of the water of gnosis."
But by means of the consecration, one immediately transcends cyclic existence.

One should consecrate [the disciple] with the verse: *Oṃ aḥ phruṃ pheṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Then, having formed the *vajrasphoṭa* mudrā, one should perform the consecration of the eight places with: *Oṃ vajrakāya hūṃ aḥ svāhā*, empowering them with the previously mentioned [mantra]. One should bestow the consecration of the *vajraghaṇṭā* with the mantra beginning: *Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe raṇitapraṇite...* and so forth. Having formed the *sattvavajrī* mudrā, having contracted the two index fingers and kissed [them], one should say: *Oṃ hūṃ aḥ svāhā*. This is the consecration of the crown of the five Buddhas. Thereafter, one should bestow the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*).
Then, having gone seven steps to the east,
and having turned his robes there again and again, he returned to that very spot and performed the empowerment sequence consisting of the supreme teaching of the three vehicles.
Having shown the sequence of empowerment (*ādhiṣṭhānakrama*) and the non-sequence (*anakrama*), he should cause [the disciple] to enter the other in due order.
Then, the disciple should give as a teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*) whatever is most desired; and it has been said:
Whatever is most beloved, whatever is most excellent—
Or indeed,
that very thing should be given as double; for one who desires that it be inexhaustible,
[it should be given] in this verse.
Thus [it is said].

Then one should begin the worship of the Vīracakra. In this regard, the procedure is as follows: having prepared a seat of various and manifold designs by encircling it with eight directions, and having placed therein the deity situated within the inner circle (aticakra), [one should offer] various flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, and diverse kinds of food and drink.
[The gift of] clothing, ornaments, and so forth, according to one's means. (yathāvibhavataḥ) [MS,
°vibhavāto MS]

Having first closed [the eyes], one should worship the *vīracakra* with the five offerings and so forth; then, having purified and consecrated the nectar (*amṛta*) joined with the ten substances according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should offer the pledge (*samaya*) to each [participant] individually with that same mudrā, while reciting this verse beginning with "Having seen and purified the Dharma," and other verses such as "Welcome to the Dharma. Then, preceded by the lotus-turning gesture (*kamalāvarta*) and accompanied by a prostration, one should do so with a well-composed mind and a pure heart, using the verse of the triple banner (*tripatākā*).

One who knows the mantras and tantras and has conquered the senses, having generated compassion for the entire realm of sentient beings, should practice the samaya-mudrā and mantra, and nothing else; thus he said.
2.3.139 Just as one is pure through the reality of one's conduct in every respect, so it has been said in the verse:
"By means of the mouth of the ring finger and the thumb, [one offers] to one's own deity and others."
Having tasted it like the drinking of Soma, one attains perfection through the practice of breath control;
this indeed is the Blessed One. (Verse 2.3.140)

The Blessed One reveals this for you with the words "as is comfortable" (*yathāsukham*) and so forth. Therein, "as is comfortable" means in whatever manner happiness arises. And here, by the word "happiness" (*sukha*), *brahman* is designated, because it is the supreme form of the bliss of reality—namely, *brahman*, *nirvāṇa*, and *mokṣa*. The attainment of that through the cultivation of the Vajra is the one-pointedness of the mind; therefore, this is the intended meaning: one should practice in such a way that there is no interruption of that one-pointedness.

2.3.141–145: "One should begin the external triangular altar (*vedī*) with red circles. Outside the wheel (*cakra*), having fashioned a triangular mandala with red sandalwood and other substances, one should provide an eastern entrance.
2.3.145: "With red flowers, incense," and so forth, the meaning is already explained. 2.3.147–156:

Having prepared the *bhūtabali* offering according to the previously mentioned sequence starting with "Oṃ ekavṛkṣa... and so on, and having filled the mouth with nectar (*amṛta*) while reciting "If [the deity] has been meditated upon," one should fill the mouth with the nectar mixed with the ten substances and beautiful fragrances. Then, preceded by the ritual action as desired, one should cast the offerings into the *bali*s while uttering the syllable *Phrūṃ*.
2.3.157 Having formed two vajra-fists with these [fingers], one should encircle the two ring fingers and form a chain with the two index fingers.
2.3.158 Having recited "Oṃ bhakṣaya 2 sarvayogeśvarī hūṃ hūṃ svāhā," one should offer the *bhūtabali* for the purpose of pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth.

2.3.160 Now, regarding the specific modes of worship: "Free from the distinctions of ritual rules and non-rules"—one should perform the special samaya-worship with a pure nature that is devoid of the conceptualization of what is edible and what is inedible.

2.3.161 One should prepare the five *tattvas* by means of the five hooks (*pañcāṅkuśa*). By the term "five hooks" and so forth, one should prepare the five *tattvas*, which are the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) whose characteristics will be described hereafter.
Thus, [31] the five...

The meaning is that one should meditate [on them] as being of the nature of the five Buddhas. Regarding "of those named Mahākuśa," this refers to human flesh. Regarding "the gnosis deity," this refers to Vairocana; the meaning is that it is desired because it possesses that intrinsic nature. Regarding "Vajrāṅkuśa," this refers to Akṣobhya; elephant flesh has the intrinsic nature of Akṣobhya. Regarding "Sthānāṅkuśa," this refers to Ratnasaṃbhava; dog flesh has the state of being the Lord of Jewels (Ratneśvara).

2.3.163 Regarding *Amogharājāṅkuśa*: "Possessing a cow" (*gomān*) refers to Amitābha, whose intrinsic nature is Amoghasiddhi; "possessing a horse" (*aśvamān*) refers to the five hooks (*pañcāṅkuśa*), whose intrinsic nature is Amitābha. These and others are for the purpose of the reality of all things (*sarvatattva*). And "the reality of all things" (*sarvatattva*) is *nirvāṇa*; its "purpose" (*prayojana*) means its cause.
2.3.164 Furthermore, these are Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, [Amitābha].
(MS: *amitābhaḥ*; MS: *ami* + *bhaḥ*)

[It is] of the nature of Amoghasiddhi (2.3.164). "That is desired by all the gods" means that, because it possesses the nature of the five Buddhas, it is most highly esteemed; that alone is appropriate for pleasing all the Yoginīs, and not [the practice of] those who delight in sensual pleasure, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "as one pleases," this is clear here. [End of manuscript fragment].
And it has been explained [in the following]:

"In its center... (2.3.165). One should employ the vowels (*ali*) and consonants (*kāli*), meaning that when the *vīracakra* is perfectly purified through the employment of the vowels and consonants according to the characteristics to be described, one should perform the yoga of non-dual union (*advayasamāpatti*). This is the intended meaning.

(2.3.166) "By the employment of the vowels and consonants, one should please all the deities. By that very employment, having performed the secret worship (*guhyapūjā*) which is the pleasing of all the Buddhas, one brings them satisfaction.
One should satisfy [the deity] thus: having extracted the nectar from its center by means of the center, one should savor it all. This is the nature of that practice;
this is the nature of that practice.
The meaning is that, having extracted the deceased, one should satisfy [the deities] by partaking of [them] with all the Yoginīs.

Regarding "of all things, beginning with the remnants" (2.3.167–176): this refers to what has been consumed in the Vīracakra, that is to say, the remains of what was drunk. "One should apply the external mandala": one should offer the offering of leavings (ucchiṣṭabali) outside the mandala at a crossroads or similar location. There, in this sequence, according to the verse:
Having personally formed the vajra-fist (*vajramuṣṭi*) and slightly bent the two index fingers raised upward, one should say "draṃ" and join them in the form of fangs (*daṃṣṭrā*).
Thus: Oṃ kuru 2 vatali mahāvatali siddhimukhi smaśānavāsinī pretamukhī caṇḍakarāli rudhirapriye samayārakṣitayogadhari yogadhari.

"O messenger of the host of *grahas*, you who have smoke for your garment, O fierce and terrible one, eat, devour! Stay! Accept, accept! *Hūṃ*! Seize, seize all the wicked! Devour, devour! *Hoḥ phruṃ pheṃ phaṭ svāhā!* Having worshipped with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) and offered the *tṛcchoṭi* [the three-snap gesture], one should dismiss [the deity]. Then, taking up the vajra and bell, [one recites] the song of the syllable *hūṃ*, which takes the form of the entire circle of heroes (*vīracakra*) and is filled with auspicious sounds."

Having praised [the deity] with this procedure by means of various vajra-songs and hymns such as "Prostrate with devotion and liberation from conceptualization" (*bhāvavimuktita*), and having worshipped with twenty offerings, one should praise [them] with the eight hundred names beginning with "O Primordial Great Being" (*paramādya mahāsattva*). Having offered the *argha* water and dedicated the merit, one should make this request: "May you forgive all that ritual which has not been performed by me. [32] Thus, one should request forgiveness.

Having made this request and forming the vajra-añjali at the heart, one makes the aspiration for the sake of liberating the entire realm of sentient beings without exception, saying, "May all sentient beings be happy," and so forth; with this, one should urge [the deity] to depart:
"The welfare of all sentient beings has been accomplished for you; the accomplishments have been granted according to their needs."
"Go to the domain of the Buddha; you shall return again," [he says] with this verse.

Placing the left vajra-fist at the heart and extending the right hand to touch the ground, he should dismiss [the deity] with this: *oṃ ātma tiṣṭha hūṃ svāhā*. Afterwards, by means of one's own breath, one's own body dissolves. Afterwards, by means of that very same breath, one causes it to enter into a friend and dissolve. The meaning is that one should bring about a state of complete merging like milk and water. And so it has been said:
Whether standing or sitting, or walking back and forth.
Whether laughing or imagining in whatever way, wherever he may be situated—
whatever [object] comes within the range of his senses.
By means of that very nature,
through the yoga of non-concentration, one should bring forth all the Buddhas.
Regarding the verse:

"One should worship by means of the yoga of instantaneous appearance, not through one's own [limited] nature"—this means that having meditated upon oneself as being of the nature of Jñānaḍākinī, and having worshipped with the five offerings and so forth, performed the eight-limbed ritual (*aṣṭāṅga-kalana*), and shown the pledge (*samaya*) as before, one should then likewise worship the external deities and perform the rite of liberation (*mokṣaṇa*) by means of this. ||o||
2.3.col. In the *Catuṣpīṭhaloka*, the third chapter, concerning the procedure for the mandala on the supreme seat (*parapīṭha*), is completed. ||~|| oṃ ||

2.4.1 Now, Vajrapāṇi, desiring to understand the specific nature of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five unwholesome acts (pañcākuśala), the vowels and consonants (alikāli), the nectar-like splendor, the external mudrās, and so forth, said: "O Blessed One, O Blessed One, I wish to hear [this]."
With the words "I desire" (*icchāmi*) and so forth, he begins the fourth chapter concerning the *parapīṭha*.
2.4.4 In the east is the nectar-water of the vajra.
°vajrāmbu] MS, °vajrambu MS ~ | one attains the nature of the five [elements]; regarding this "regarding this," [it is found in] MS, iti ... MS.
"Previously" means that, at the beginning, *śukra* was explained; [this is the meaning]. *Amṛtavajrāmbu*.

"Vajrāmbu" means semen (*śukra*). "Five" means having the nature of the five [elements]. "Self" (*ātman*) means that it arises within the self; this is the meaning. It is produced again and again from the self.
"Bodhicitta consists of the five elements"—thus it is said. He explains that very point: fire is "heated" (*ūṣmāyate*);
[the term] *sparśa* (touch) refers to the state of being heated. By virtue of being heated, it is touch.
The intrinsic nature of touch is the fire element; wind is the cause of smoke,
[of smoke].

"It is seen" means that it is seen as moving upward in the form of wind; therefore, it is the element of constant motion (*satatagati*). "Water" has the nature of fluidity (*drava*); since fluidity also exists, it is the water element (*abdhātu*). "The form of earth is seen" means that because it is perceived as being composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*), it also possesses solidity (*khakkhaṭatva*); therefore, it is the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*). "By the vajra presided over by gnosis" means that because of its state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) through the nature of the gnosis of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*).
The space element: "one should meditate upon the five deities" means that one should contemplate [the body] as consisting of the five elements in the form of the five Tathāgatas.
2.4.6 "All the configuration of water perishes" means that this entire [body], primarily by way of its nature as water... [nature as water]. MS, MS.

Because it is dependently originated, that which is established as the objective support—the form of fire—is also empty, since its intrinsic nature is dependent. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that earth and the other elements likewise possess such a nature. In that very context, he states the seed-syllable to be placed: "Just as wind is among the eternal," and so forth. In this regard: "wind" (*vāyu*) refers to the letter *va*; "of the eternal" (*nityānām*) refers to the letter *ha*; "the meaning of *haṃsa*" refers to the letter *sa*; "earth" (*pṛthivī*) refers to the letter *ha*; and "witness" (*sākṣiṇa*) refers to the letter *kṣa*.
2.4.7 Having joined the *bindu* and the *nāda*,
[there are] fivefold *jñānākṣaras*. These five *dharmākṣaras* follow the *bindu* into the *nāda*, which is that letter *ū*.

The meaning is that one should join [the letter] with the syllable *ukāra*. As for the phrase "in its center, however, the nectar-syllable in the middle of the moon," the word "its" (*tasya*) means "of them. "In the middle of the moon" means in the moon situated at the center of the head; one should contemplate the drop (*bindu*), which is the transformation of the syllable *sakāra*, in the middle of that.

2.4.8 Regarding the statement "one should say 'five, five' with the vajra-water for self-purification": here, "five" refers to the nature of the five Buddhas; furthermore, "five" should be said to refer to the five seed-syllables. Having recited this, "vajra-water" refers to semen (*śukra*), and "for self-purification" means for the sake of purifying one's own body. "Semen consisting of the five elements" refers to the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) together with the four [deities] beginning with Vairocana, who will be described later.

One should employ [the practice] beginning with *ādinā* for the sake of awakening the body presided over by passion (*rāga*) and so forth, together with the five seeds just mentioned via the channel (*nāḍī*). Here, the purification of the nectar-syllable, which is semen alone, is taught, and not that of feces, urine, and so forth.

The essence is stated through the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), because it is the cause of the production of the three worlds. The purification of semen is taught primarily, and not that of others. And thus it has been said:
In the verse it is said: "The nectar is semen. From that, the three worlds are produced.
Thus [it is said]. Intending to explain the very meaning already stated, he says: "Therefore, it is far removed from delusion, being free from existence and non-existence.
Here, by the word *bhāva* (existence), there is the apprehension of all phenomena as having existence; and by the word *abhāva* (non-existence) as well, [there is the apprehension] of them...

The perception of those very [factors] as non-existent is "freed from" them; that is to say, it is established by their exclusion. The meaning is that, because of this, delusion and the other [afflictions] are cast far away. And it has been said in a verse:
Just as food [is offered] into the fire,
so too is the common sphere of experience.
Just as the sun makes visible what is seen, so does discernment perceive;
just as the wind carries away fragrance, so does conceptualization take hold of its own objects.
[Free from] conceptual construction,
far removed from the ocean of delusion—
this is the verse.
Thus [it is said].

2.4.9 Thus, he says that the substance, having been purified in this way, should be offered into the sacrificial pit of the stomach (*udarakuṇḍa*) by one who is free from the conceptual distinction between what is edible and what is inedible, according to the characteristics to be described. And the external nectar (*bāhyāmṛta*) of the substance is to be transformed by fire-cooking. In that context, "external nectar" refers to ghee, honey, curd, milk, sugar, and so forth; "transformed" (*vikopya*) means [subject to] transformation (*pariṇāma*).
(Note: *pariṇāmaḥ* appears twice in the manuscript.)

"Like the cooking by fire": this is the intended meaning. Just as the effect of boiled rice and so forth, produced by the cooking performed by ordinary fire, is accepted and admitted by those whose minds have not investigated the true nature [of things]; so too here, the acceptance by the wise of the effects such as feces and urine produced by the cooking of the fire of knowledge as something to be accepted is not contradictory, because all entities are delightful only when left unexamined. And it has been said in a verse: "A single entity is the intrinsic nature of all entities."
All phenomena have the single nature of being;
he by whom one phenomenon is seen in its true reality has,
by that very fact, seen all phenomena in their true reality.
Thus it is said in verse;
furthermore, it has been stated again:
It has been said: "There is nothing whatsoever that should not be done by means of wisdom and skillful means; thus [it is] for the mind."

The verse thus clarifies the meaning already stated by means of the passage beginning with "the stomach, etc., [is] fire" (*kukṣyādyājñānam agniḥ*). "Stomach" (*kukṣi*) refers to the abdomen; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the sense-bases such as the eyes are included. "Fire of knowledge" (*jñānāgni*) refers to the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*). "Remnants" (*ucchiṣṭa*) refers to the transformed excrement and urine—that is, feces and so forth. Through the cooking by the fire of knowledge, the transformed excrement, urine, and so forth, become more excellent within the stomach and other organs. Therefore... [MS, tasmāt].

One should not suspect that the offering of feces, urine, and so forth is utterly contradictory to the *bauddhas*, because it is for the purpose of abandoning conceptual constructions such as "impurity" and the like. And regarding this, it is stated in a verse of the *Māyājāla*:
"Since [the body] arises from the great elements, how can it be called impure?"
Verse 2.4.10:

"But the fire-digestion" refers to the fires; its center is the oblation. Regarding this, Vairocanādi says: "Of the fires" means of the fire of knowledge (*jñānāgni*); "its" refers to the fire of discernment (*vijñānāgni*).
One should offer [it] as an oblation into the fire of consciousness (*vijñānāgni*); one should offer [it].

This is the meaning: Just as when rice-gruel and other effects produced from fragrant *śāli* rice and so forth are assisted by an external fire, they become more excellent because they have arisen from an excellent cause; likewise here too, the effect consisting of feces, urine, and so forth—when produced with the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*) as a cooperative condition—is purified, for it has been processed in the fire like *śāli* rice and the like. Therefore, one should offer oblations of Vairocana and the others into the fire of gnosis, being free from conceptual constructions such as pure and impure.

Regarding the phrase "reciting the vajra with the seed-syllable of the vajra, and likewise with the seed-syllable," the term "vajra" here means the vajra meditated upon within the center of the fire-pit (udarakuṇḍa). "Reciting the vajra with the seed-syllable of the vajra" means revolving the syllable *hūṃ*; that is to say, one should meditate on the syllable *hūṃ* within the central hub (*varaṭaka*) of the vajra, which is what is meant by "with the seed-syllable."

2.4.11 "In its center, one should contemplate the flame-sun as the syllable *cic*. This means that by means of the syllable *cic*, one should contemplate the nature of the flame-sun; having contemplated the terrible *ḍākinī*, one should offer oblations into the midst of that flame-sun.
2.4.12 The passage beginning with "Padmeśvara" and so forth has already been explained.

2.4.15 Now, because it is produced from wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), it has the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; therefore, it is designated by the word "vajra. He says: "Ali means a bee. Here, "ali" means "bee," which is a synonym for Vajrabhairava. He states that its pervasiveness is all-encompassing, like the limit of space, by virtue of having the *dharmadhātu* as its nature: "Ali, extending to the limits of space, has the *dharmadhātu* as its nature."

2.4.16 *Sakalotpannadehānāṃ sacara guhyadhṛk*. Because it is to be held by the *sakalas* (those possessing all parts) through their secret nature (*guhyasvabhāva*) in the form of the secret (*guhyarūpeṇa*), it is the "holder of the secret" (*guhyadhṛk*). And that is the nectar (*amṛta*). It is in the eighteen limbs (*aṣṭādaśa-m-aṅge*), meaning it is established in the eighteen locations beginning with the breasts. For this very reason he says: *Amṛta sarvam indriyam*, meaning it is "taste" (*svāda*) because it abides in all the sense organs (*sarvendriya*).

2.4.17. "But having drawn it from the center of that, one dissolves it into the midst of the *ali* (vowels). This means: having drawn it from that sense-faculty (*indriya*), one should place it in the midst of the *ali*. The meaning is: having withdrawn it from the eighteen locations, one should produce the hundred signs (*nimitta*). "Bhairava" refers to the vajra-amṛta; its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is such that it becomes Bhairava, for it fills [all things] by way of the nature of nectar (*amṛta*). It sustains all sentient beings (*satvāni*).

He supports and plays excessively; he dwells by pervading the three realms. He is called *bhairava* because, as stated in the verse, he "supports" (*bhara-ti*) and "plays" (*ram-a-ti*) everywhere and at all times.
Because it dwells within all, it is therefore called *bhairava* in the verse.

Regarding "Vajranāda," the syllable *hūṃ* arises; having filled [the space] with the resonance of the *hūṃ*, one should generate [it], like a substance for yoga, through the process of gradual accomplishment. Thus, the nature of the Supreme Brahman is born. And it has been said:
Through the union of the vajra and the lotus, one shall become equal to Vajrasattva.
Thus [it is said]. 2.4.18 To explain the nature of the *vajranāda*, he says: "wind and fire," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.

2.4.19 Regarding "the seed preceded by the vowel," this refers to the letter *a*. "One should hold it in its center" means that within the center of that *vajra*, one should cause the letter *hūṃ*—which has become liquefied from the letter *a*—to abide upon the lunar disc.

2.4.20 Having explained the nature of *ali*, he now speaks in order to explain the nature of *kāli*: "The flower is known as *kāli*. In that context, *kāli* is the *dharmodaya*; "the knowledge of the flower" means that very flower is what is known. As for "the Vajrin whose form is the flower," because it has the nature of the lotus (*padma*), the *vajra* possesses a form therein; for this very reason, it is designated by the word *ali*. She is the "Mother in all births within saṃsāra"; she is the "Mother of all beings" because she is the progenitor of all those who fall within the bounds of saṃsāra.

For this very reason, it is specified as "of all the stages" (*sarvabhūmīnām*), because it is the place of origin for all of them. Furthermore, qualifying it once more, he says: "This ocean of the water of knowledge, with the crocodiles and fish of wisdom. In that context, "the water of knowledge" refers to the ocean of water.

"Samudra" means "ocean," filled with the water of immortality (*amṛta*). It is an ocean because it is the abode of the jewel of bodhicitta, endowed with various skillful means (*upāya*), which serves as the cause for the reality of the Vajradhara-nature. Regarding the phrase "by the crocodiles and fish of wisdom (*prajñā*)," wisdom is expressed by the word *prajñā* because it possesses the power to rescue the entire realm of sentient beings from saṃsāra; and that [wisdom] takes various forms such as crocodiles, fish, and so forth. In the phrase "in the midst of the mud of non-duality, by the sprout of skillful means (*upāya*)," "non-duality" refers to the union, which is the lotus; this is the sign of skillful means. That very thing is what is meant by "the sprout."

2.4.22 With the words "resembling a blooming bandhūka flower," etc., he explains the division of colors for that very [lotus]. "Madhu is the abode of nectar" means that its nature is honey; the meaning is "the abode of nectar. "Kālī is the nectar of that very [lotus]" means that because she is the support (*ādhāra*) of that nectar, Kālī also has the nature of nectar. Having thus visualized the lotus, he asks: "How should one cause it to bloom? He says: "The unfolding is the flower, the water is the cloud. In this context, "unfolding" (*vivarta*) means causing to bloom;
"flower" (*puṣpa*) means the lotus. [MS: *asya padmam*] MS, *padma + sya* MS.

"Viśeṣa-ambuṣa" refers to the lotus flower; "the secret [lotus] called paṅkaja" is what is meant. (2.4.23) He asks, "By what should one cause it to blossom? and replies with the words beginning "dviguṇākṣara. In that context, "dviguṇākṣara" refers to the letter *kṣa*. "Of the *bindus*" refers to the form of the half-moon on its head; that is the line of the *bindu*. "One should join it at the base with the *nāda*" means union with the vowel *u*. This is the meaning: one should place the seed-syllable of the *yoni* in the center of the moon-maṇḍala transformed from the letter *a* within the interior of the lotus. Of that syllable-seed... [36] ...of that syllable-seed.

Regarding the seed-syllable: "the deities are the Kula-mothers"—this refers to the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of that seed-syllable. It means that [the syllable] is transformed into the very form of the terrible *Ḍākinī*. As for the term "Kula-mothers," the meaning is that upon such accomplishment, one attains the state of being a Kula-mother. And it is said in the verse:
"Tārā, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, Māmakī, and Buddhalocanā."
These five are the family mothers of the goddess Prajñāpāramitā, as stated in the verse.

2.4.24 "Having meditated upon the seed-syllable of nectar (amṛtabīja) within the moon, it is thus contemplated. This means that one should further visualize the syllable *A* upon the moon produced from the *A* of the *dharmodayā* of the goddesses as well.

2.4.25 "They say *ali* means 'bee' (*bhramara*)," and likewise for the *Tathāgatī*. Just as the word *bhramara* is expressed by the meaning of the word *ali*, so too the word *tathāgata-puṣpa* has the same meaning. Thus, [it refers to] the *Tathāgatī*. Here, the procedure for the nectar arising from the production of both is stated.

"Both" means: "arising from wisdom and method"—this refers to the activity, and this is the underlying intention. That which is being produced through the union of wisdom and method, the most distinguished effect of the vajra-amṛta, is designated by the term "attainment" (*siddhi*). Therefore, here too, [it is] wisdom and method...
[The union of] wisdom and means;
arisen through the conjunction of the lotus and the vajra; the nectar of semen, the nectar of semen.
Because it is the cause of that Nirvana,
it is called by the word "immortal" (*amṛta*), through the metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause.
2.4.26 And because that [mantra] consists of the nature of the deity, it is the syllable of Dharma. He says:
"The third of each group," and so forth. Of the third letters of each group, it is grasped by three syllables; thus, the letter *ḍa* is the staff (*daṇḍa*).

Regarding "of the vajras [measuring] a staff-length" (*daṇḍamātrasya vajrāṇām*): one should place a form shaped like the letter *repha*, measuring a staff-length, at its side, and encircle it with girdles (*mekhalā*) and so forth.

It should be recited thus: "In each of those [positions], there is a line in the shape of a girdle (*mekhalā*); when joined, this is the letter *a*. Indeed, the letter *a* is the cause for the arising of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*); and so it is well-established in all tantras."
The syllable *a* is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are unarisen from the very beginning.
Thus it is said [in the text], 2.4.27–28: "By these [elements], in due order, the state of the five nectars (pañcāmṛtatva) is declared.
[MS: pañcāmṛtatvam; MS: pañcāmṛtatatvam].

Thus, in this context, "by these" refers to the letter *a*. Because it is perfected by the letter *a*, it is the reality (*tattva*) of the five nectars, such as semen and so forth; the meaning is that they are to be meditated upon as having the nature of the five Tathāgatas. Alternatively, the letter *a* itself is the reality of the five nectars. For this very reason, he says that it is suitable for the removal of the views of self and so forth held by those with wrong views. [He states: "It is the washing away of the self for embodied beings," and "By means of these nectars, they know the five nectars specifically."

Regarding the specific nature of that which is called *amṛta* (nectar), namely semen (*śukra*), and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*): it is said that those who know these see the paths of the Tathāgatas and the Tathāgatas themselves. Having "observed the gateways to the [various] destinies" means: whatever belongs to the pure body at any point on the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)—that is, of the pure body—is Buddhahood, the state of holding the Vajra (*vajradharatva*).

The meaning is: "or may they attain [it]. Explaining this very point, he says: "The nectar of yoga, when known, is tasted by the flavor of nectar. Thus, the purification of blood and the other [substances] must be performed. Now, in order to explain the distinction between the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five unwholesome foods (*pañcākuśa*), he says: "Listen, O Vajra, to the reality as it is, especially regarding the five foods. And how is it that these ten substances are called "the five foods"? Because they are employed by being unified through the state of five-fifths, there are five sets of five foods.

Regarding the "edibles" that have been mentioned: "By whom it should be known, he would eat; the state is swiftly shown"—here, "by whom" means by the practitioner (*sādhaka*), having meditated upon his own essential nature (*svarūpa*). If this is practiced, "the state is swiftly shown" means that by means of that, one has quickly attained the state of Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). 2.4.30 *Mahāmati* refers to semen (*śukra*); *vākya* refers to blood (*rakta*); *sajāti* refers to adamantine water (*vajrodaka*); *sṛṣṭavīraka* refers to Vairocana. "It should be consumed with crystal" means it should be practiced with a pure nature free from the conceptual constructions of what is to be grasped and what is not to be grasped. *Mahākuśita*.
"Mahākuśita" [MS], "mahākusita" [MS] means *mahāmāṃsa* (great flesh). "Of the yogins" (*yoginām*) means "by the yogins. 2.4.31.

Regarding "the recitation of the seed-syllable born from consciousness" (*vijñānabījajāpa*), "its seed is that which sustains" (*tasya bījan tu dhāriṇam*): in that phrase "seed of consciousness," the letter *a* is the seed; "recitation of the five nectars" (*pañcāmṛta-jāpanam*) is fully accomplished through that, meaning one should recite with great care. "The dharma-syllable of the five hooks" (*pañcāṅkuśasya dharmākṣaram*) refers to what was previously stated.

2.4.32 Now he states the introduction for the sake of its purification: "One should apply the goad of that obstacle to its limb," and so forth. In this context, "the goad of obstacles" refers to elephant flesh; "one should purify with the syllable *hūṃ*. 2.4.33 "The goad of the place" refers to dog flesh; saying "one should purify with the syllable *ghrīṃ*," he speaks. 2.4.34 One should join horse flesh with the syllable *jrīṃ*.
He makes it clear [with the words] "yojayet" (one should join) and "iti" (thus).

With the passage beginning "adhiṣṭhata hayāṅkuśa" (2.4.35), he indicates that one should differentiate by means of the syllable *sriī* (the seed-syllable of the cow). Therein, "the *vajra*-tattva" is so called because its intrinsic nature is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); "the *ghaṇṭā*-tattva" is so called because it conforms to resonance, meaning that its intrinsic nature is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); "the *akṣasūtra*-tattva" means that it is to be cultivated as the intrinsic nature of all the Tathāgatas; and "the *jñāna*-tattva" refers to one who knows the nature of things as they truly abide, to the highest limit—that *tattva*, and he who knows it, attains unsurpassed nirvāṇa.

3.4.1 Now, regarding the application of the vajra-bell and so forth, as well as the flowers, incense, and so forth—how are these to be joined non-dually? With the words beginning "Vajrapāṇi has entered into a state of curiosity to hear," [the author] requests Vajrapāṇi to explain this.

3.4.2 Demonstrating through the yoga of the equality of all phenomena by way of being free from the conceptualization of subject and object, he says: "Listen, O Vajra, how success arises from the reality of non-dual yoga. The meaning is that one should meditate upon the vajra, bell, and so forth, which have been taught through visualization, according to the illustration that will be explained.

3.4.3 How one should meditate is stated as follows: "One should hold oneself as the vajra by way of reality, and the bell as the Dharma. In that context, regarding "holding oneself as the vajra by way of reality": when analyzed according to ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), because it is to be offered up, one's own aggregate (*skandha*) itself becomes the vajra. It is a vajra because its intrinsic nature is emptiness like a vajra, and because it is indestructible. Regarding "the bell as the Dharma": because its essential nature is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the bell, which is its very nature, represents wisdom.

The *mudrā* is that into which one dissolves through the yoga of the *saṃpuṭa*; thus, "the yoga of the *saṃpuṭa*" refers to the union of the *vajra* and the *padma*, and that is the meeting of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). For this very reason, it is said: "one dissolves into its means. That itself is the intrinsic nature of all *mudrās*. Thus it has been stated in the *Śrīsamāja*:
[verse on] hand-mudrās... [is not].

It is the forbearance of one who is capable of enduring the striking of swords and weapons. Just as there is a distinction between loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*), so too [is there a distinction here].

Regarding verse 3.4.17, he asks: "Having relied upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*), how should one stand? On the full breasts, on the tips of the hands, on the neck, as well as on the lower lip, at the base of the cheeks, eyes, and ears, on the head, and indeed on every limb.
In the bright fortnight all is thus; in the dark fortnight it is said to be the reverse. [The letter] *a* is at the base of the thumb, and *ā* is at the base of the thumb.
The letter *i* is on the two shanks; the letter *ī* is situated in the pair of thighs;
the letter *u* is at the base of the navel, and likewise the letter *ū* is in the abdomen.
The letter *ṛ* is at the base of the breasts, while the letter *ṝ* is situated on the hands;
the letter *ḷ* is on the throat, and likewise the letter *ḹ* is on the head.
The letter *e* is on the region of the cheeks, and the letter *ai* is on the two eyes.
One should apply the ritual procedures: the syllable *oṃ* at the root of the ear, the syllable *au* situated on the crown of the head, and *aṃ* and *aḥ* for the body comprising all limbs;
[these include] kissing, embracing, and so forth, as well as biting and clinging.
One should apply the locations according to their forms and contemplate them as having the shape of the god of love (Smara).
By merely contemplating in this way, women are satisfied, and not otherwise;
even without the union of the female organ and the male organ, O fair-faced one.
